labs.focus: Learn to read a Mishnah that counts cases before the Gemara begins its analysis.

steps.title: What is this Mishnah organizing?
steps.hebrew: יציאות השבת שתים שהן ארבע בפנים ושתים שהן ארבע בחוץ
steps.translation: The acts of carrying out on Shabbat are two that are four inside, and two that are four outside.
steps.prompt: Before reaching for every detail, identify the job of the opening line.
answers: It introduces a counted set of cases that the Mishnah will distinguish.
It gives a short narrative story about a certain person who had once forgotten that it was Shabbat.
It announces a single final ruling directly and immediately, without laying out any underlying cases.
steps.feedback: Good. The Mishnah opens by organizing a legal field through numbered cases.

steps.title: Notice the two locations
steps.translation: Inside · outside
steps.prompt: What distinction will matter as the Mishnah develops its cases?
answers: Whether the action is inside or outside a domain.
Whether the action happens in the morning or evening.
Whether the person is rich or poor.
steps.feedback: Exactly. The terms mark the two sides of the exchange the Mishnah is about to describe.

steps.title: A counted Mishnah needs examples
steps.translation: Two that are four
steps.prompt: Why might a Mishnah use the phrase “two that are four”?
answers: It signals basic cases and related extensions that require careful sorting.
It means that only two cases genuinely exist here, and that all of the rest simply do not matter at all.
It is telling the reader that they may simply skip right over the accompanying examples entirely.
steps.feedback: Right. The phrase prepares the learner to track how a compact principle unfolds into cases.

steps.title: Why two becomes four
steps.translation: The poor person · the householder.
steps.prompt: The Mishnah says 'two that are four.' What doubles the count from two to four?
answers: Each basic transfer is counted from two sides -- the poor person outside and the householder inside -- so two acts yield four liable cases.
The Mishnah is simply listing four completely unrelated Shabbat prohibitions that just happen to be grouped together in one place.
The number four here refers to the four cups of wine, a detail brought in from an entirely different and unrelated area of law.
steps.feedback: Right. 'Two that are four' means each act of transfer is seen from both the giver's and the receiver's side, doubling two core cases into four.

steps.title: Recall, don't just recognize
steps.translation: carrying out, from one domain to another.
steps.prompt: Type the English meaning of הוֹצָאָה (hotza'ah) from memory, in a few words.
acceptable: taking out from one domain to another
carrying from one domain to another
steps.feedback: Typing it from memory beats recognizing it. Hotza'ah -- carrying or transferring between domains -- is the melacha this whole opening Mishnah counts.

labs.focus: Use a concise Mishnah to separate the action, its time, and the tool used to perform it.

steps.title: Begin with the verb
steps.hebrew: אור לארבעה עשר בודקין את החמץ לאור הנר
steps.translation: On the eve of the fourteenth, one searches for leaven by the light of a lamp.
steps.prompt: What does the Mishnah tell a person to do?
answers: Search for chametz.
Eat the Passover offering.
Recite the evening Shema.
steps.feedback: Correct. First identify the required action before analyzing its timing or details.

steps.title: Read time and tool separately
steps.translation: On the eve of the fourteenth · by the light of a lamp
steps.prompt: Which pairing correctly identifies the two supporting details?
answers: The first phrase gives the time; the second gives the tool.
The first gives the tool; the second gives the time.
Both phrases give different names for chametz.
steps.feedback: Yes. This is a core close-reading habit: separate action, time, and instrument.

steps.title: Where might Gemara focus?
steps.translation: Light / the eve
steps.prompt: A short opening word can carry more than one shade of meaning. What is a responsible next question?
answers: What does this word mean here, and how does the surrounding Mishnah clarify it?
Which of the later laws should we simply decide upon now, without first reading through the discussion?
Can we simply ignore the word altogether, on the grounds that the required action itself is already clear?
steps.feedback: Exactly. Gemara often slows down over a compact word and tests it against the context and sources.

steps.title: Why one word decides the law
steps.translation: 'Or' -- does it mean daytime, or the evening?
steps.prompt: The Gemara opens by asking what 'or' means. Why does that single word matter so much?
answers: The whole timing of the mitzvah depends on it -- if 'or' means the evening, the search begins on the night of the fourteenth rather than by day.
It matters only for the correct pronunciation of the Mishnah when it is read aloud, but has no real effect at all on the practical law.
The word decides which kind of lamp is kosher for the search, distinguishing an ordinary oil lamp from a wax candle for the purpose.
steps.feedback: Right. The Gemara slows down on 'or' precisely because the practical time to search for chametz turns entirely on whether it means day or night.

steps.title: Recall, don't just recognize
steps.translation: leaven.
steps.prompt: Type the English meaning of חָמֵץ (chametz) from memory, in a word or two.
steps.feedback: Typing it from memory beats recognizing it. Chametz -- leaven -- is the object of the search this Mishnah requires on the eve of the fourteenth.

labs.focus: Learn to separate a Mishnah’s physical description from the legal question it invites.

steps.title: Find the object under discussion
steps.hebrew: מָבוֹי שֶׁהוּא גָבוֹהַּ לְמַעְלָה מֵעֶשְׂרִים אַמָּה
steps.translation: An alleyway whose entrance is higher than twenty cubits.
steps.prompt: What fact does the Mishnah give before stating what should be done?
answers: The height of an alleyway entrance.
The time for evening Shema.
The ownership of a lost object.
steps.feedback: Exactly. Start by locating the concrete case before looking for the rule.

steps.title: Notice the Mishnah’s instruction
steps.translation: One should lower it.
steps.prompt: What kind of move is this short word making?
answers: It gives the required response to the case.
It asks for a biblical proof.
It introduces a disagreement between witnesses.
steps.feedback: Right. A compact Mishnah often gives the case and its response before explaining why.

steps.title: Ask the next responsible question
steps.translation: Why?
steps.prompt: What question naturally opens the Gemara’s analysis of this Mishnah?
answers: Why does this measurement determine the response?
Who was the very first person that originally built this particular alleyway long ago?
Which single Hebrew letter happens to appear the most often across this line of text?
steps.feedback: Yes. Gemara turns a terse threshold into an inquiry about the reason and source of the rule.

steps.title: What the height threshold protects
steps.translation: The crossbeam · the visible marker.
steps.prompt: Why should an alleyway entrance higher than twenty cubits be lowered?
answers: Above twenty cubits the eye no longer notices the crossbeam marking the entrance, so the alley fails to register as an enclosed doorway.
Because an entrance built that tall would be structurally unstable and might well collapse onto the people who pass by beneath it.
Because the Torah itself fixes twenty cubits as the maximum lawful height for any kind of structure built anywhere in a city.
steps.feedback: Right. The measure is about perception: a marker too high to be noticed cannot do its legal work of defining the alleyway. Sukkah's twenty-cubit limit turns on the very same idea.

steps.title: Recall, don't just recognize
steps.translation: an alleyway.
steps.prompt: Type the English meaning of מָבוֹי (mavoi) from memory, in a word or two.
steps.feedback: Typing it from memory beats recognizing it. The mavoi -- a shared alleyway -- is the physical space whose enclosure this whole opening sugya is about.

labs.focus: Enter a civil-law sugya by identifying the conflict, the claims, and the evidence question.

steps.title: Two people, one garment
steps.translation: Two people are holding a garment.
steps.prompt: What basic situation does the Mishnah place before the reader?
answers: Two people make competing claims over the same object.
Two people agree to divide a gift equally.
A merchant is measuring cloth for sale.
steps.feedback: Correct. Start with the human and legal conflict before parsing the remedies.

steps.title: Each person says: I found it
steps.hebrew: זה אומר אני מצאתיה וזה אומר אני מצאתיה
steps.translation: This one says, “I found it,” and this one says, “I found it.”
steps.prompt: Why does the Mishnah repeat the same claim from both sides?
answers: It establishes that neither side’s assertion alone settles the dispute.
It sets out to prove that the very first person to make the claim here is the one who is correct.
It quietly changes the case into a question about the laws of ritual purity rather than ownership.
steps.feedback: Yes. Parallel claims create the evidentiary problem the Mishnah must address.

steps.title: What must the court decide?
steps.translation: They divide [it].
steps.prompt: Before treating a short ruling as simple, what should a learner ask?
answers: What facts, claims, and legal principles make this response appropriate?
Which one of the two claimants here comes across as the more personally sympathetic figure?
Whether this Mishnah is really only telling a simple story rather than actually stating a law.
steps.feedback: Exactly. The Gemara’s work is to test how and why a terse Mishnah response follows from its case.

steps.title: Why divide, rather than choose
steps.translation: Physical possession · an oath.
steps.prompt: Why does the Mishnah resolve two equal claimants by having them divide, rather than picking one?
answers: Each is physically grasping the cloak, so each has a possession claim to at least half; with no basis to prefer either, the court divides it under oath.
The court divides it simply because dividing any disputed object exactly in half is always the automatic default rule in every single monetary dispute.
Because splitting the object evenly is just the most peaceful available outcome, chosen only to avoid a quarrel rather than for any real legal reason.
steps.feedback: Right. The division rests on each party's grip: possession gives each a claim to half, and an oath backs it. It is not a generic 'split everything' rule.

steps.title: Recall, don't just recognize
steps.translation: they shall divide it.
steps.prompt: Type the English meaning of יַחֲלוֹקוּ (yachloku) from memory, in a few words.
steps.feedback: Typing it from memory beats recognizing it. Yachloku -- 'they shall divide it' -- is the terse ruling whose reasoning the entire sugya then unpacks.

labs.focus: Read a Mishnah that gives a physical limit, then ask what makes that limit meaningful.

steps.title: What is being measured?
steps.hebrew: סֻכָּה שֶׁהִיא גְבוֹהָה לְמַעְלָה מֵעֶשְׂרִים אַמָּה
steps.translation: A sukkah that is higher than twenty cubits.
steps.prompt: What concrete feature does the Mishnah place before the reader?
answers: The height of a sukkah.
The time of a festival meal.
The owner of a field.
steps.feedback: Good. Begin with the physical case before asking why the measure matters.

steps.title: What does the Mishnah say?
steps.translation: It is invalid.
steps.prompt: What kind of statement is this?
answers: A ruling about the described case.
A question about a verse.
A description of a custom.
steps.feedback: Exactly. The Mishnah’s short ruling gives the Gemara something precise to investigate.

steps.title: What comes next?
steps.translation: What is the reason?
steps.prompt: What productive question does this phrase invite?
answers: Why does this height affect the validity of the sukkah?
Who was the very first person ever to build a sukkah in all of history?
Which single one of these particular words is by far the easiest one to translate?
steps.feedback: Right. A measurement becomes a Gemara question when the reader asks what principle explains it.

steps.title: Three reasons, one purpose
steps.translation: The covering (sechach) · a temporary dwelling.
steps.prompt: The Gemara gives three reasons why a too-tall sukkah is invalid. What do they share?
answers: Each ties the limit to the sukkah's purpose -- that a person notice the sechach overhead and dwell in a temporary booth, not a permanent house.
Each of the three separate reasons depends entirely on the specific building materials that were used to construct the sukkah's walls.
They all agree that the number twenty was simply handed down at Sinai with no underlying reason ever made available to us at all.
steps.feedback: Right. All three reasons connect the measure back to what a sukkah is for -- a noticed covering and a temporary dwelling. Eruvin's alleyway limit runs on the same perception logic.

steps.title: Recall, don't just recognize
steps.translation: it is invalid.
steps.prompt: Type the English meaning of פְּסוּלָה (pesulah) from memory, in a word or two.
steps.feedback: Typing it from memory beats recognizing it. Pesulah -- 'it is invalid' -- is the Mishnah's terse ruling that the Gemara's three reasons then set out to explain.

labs.focus: Separate a Mishnah’s schedule from the social and legal reason the Gemara will examine.

steps.title: Read the schedule
steps.translation: A virgin is married on Wednesday.
steps.prompt: What kind of information does the opening line provide?
answers: A scheduled time for a case.
A list of witnesses.
A biblical quotation.
steps.feedback: Yes. First identify that the Mishnah is setting a time before pursuing the reason.

steps.title: A schedule invites explanation
steps.translation: Why specifically Wednesday?
steps.prompt: What is the Gemara likely to investigate?
answers: Why this particular day serves the Mishnah’s concern.
How exactly one is supposed to correctly spell out the word Wednesday in Hebrew.
Whether or not this particular Mishnah happens to have been given a page number.
steps.feedback: Exactly. The Gemara often turns a fixed detail into a question about institutional purpose.

steps.title: Keep the structure visible
steps.translation: Mishnah · question · reason
steps.prompt: Which sequence describes this opening?
answers: A schedule, a question about it, then an explanation.
A single final ruling stated outright at once, with no further discussion of it at all.
A biblical verse, followed immediately afterward by an entirely unrelated narrative story.
steps.feedback: Good. You are tracking the function of each line, not only its vocabulary.

steps.title: A schedule built around a court
steps.translation: That [courts] were in session · a claim about virginity.
steps.prompt: Why did the Sages set the wedding of a virgin specifically for Wednesday?
answers: Courts sat on Thursday, so a groom disputing her virginity could reach court the very next morning, before his anger cooled and he stayed silent.
Wednesday simply happened to be the least busy market day of the entire week, which made it far more convenient for the two families to gather.
The Torah itself explicitly commands that all weddings must take place at the exact midpoint of the week, and Wednesday is precisely that day.
steps.feedback: Right. The Wednesday schedule is engineered around the Thursday court, so a virginity claim can be raised at once rather than lost to delay -- the schedule serves a legal purpose.

steps.title: Recall, don't just recognize
steps.translation: a virgin.
steps.prompt: Type the English meaning of בְּתוּלָה (betulah) from memory, in a word or two.
steps.feedback: Typing it from memory beats recognizing it. Betulah -- 'a virgin' -- is the status whose marriage day, and the reason behind it, this opening Mishnah fixes.

labs.focus: Enter a damages sugya by recognizing how a Mishnah organizes categories before it debates their details.

steps.title: The Mishnah opens with a list
steps.translation: There are four primary categories of damages.
steps.prompt: What is the Mishnah doing with this opening phrase?
answers: Organizing a legal field into foundational categories.
Recounting a story about four people who caused damage.
Delivering one final ruling about how damages are paid.
steps.feedback: Correct. A numbered opening tells the learner to expect distinctions and examples, not a narrative or a single verdict.

steps.title: What is an av?
steps.translation: Primary categories.
steps.prompt: Why might the Mishnah call these categories avot, “fathers”?
answers: They are root cases from which related cases can be understood.
They are the proper names of the figures who first taught them.
They are a signal that the tractate's discussion has now concluded.
steps.feedback: Exactly. The term prepares the reader for a system of root-and-derivative cases, not proper names or a closing marker.

steps.title: What will Gemara ask?
steps.translation: What is different?
steps.prompt: What reasoning task fits a list of legal categories?
answers: Compare what distinguishes one category from another.
Rank the four categories from most to least severe.
Determine which single category the other three derive from.
steps.feedback: Right. Gemara examines why categories are alike or different and what follows from that — not a severity ranking, and no one category generates the others.

steps.title: Not one is like another
steps.translation: The ox is not like the maveh.
steps.prompt: The Mishnah spends its next lines saying what each category is NOT like the others. Why open by stressing differences?
answers: Because you cannot responsibly group cases together until you know exactly where they differ.
Because the categories turn out to have nothing in common at all.
Because the Torah listed them separately and they may never be compared.
steps.feedback: Good. The lo-harei lines build toward a shared side precisely by first ruling out that any one category could stand in for the others.

steps.title: After the differences, a common thread
steps.hebrew: הַצַּד הַשָּׁוֶה שֶׁבָּהֶן שֶׁדַּרְכָּן לְהַזִּיק וּשְׁמִירָתָן עָלֶיךָ
steps.translation: Their shared side: their way is to cause damage, and guarding them is your responsibility.
steps.prompt: After ruling out sameness, the Mishnah names what all four DO share. What has the Mishnah accomplished?
answers: It turned four differentiated cases into one legal field held together by a single principle of responsibility.
It cancelled the very differences it had just so carefully drawn between the four separate categories.
It quietly selected the strongest of the four categories to serve as the governing model for the rest.
steps.feedback: Exactly. Differentiate, then unify — the tzad hashaveh is what lets four distinct damagers carry one shared consequence.

steps.title: Recall, don't just recognize
steps.translation: There are four primary categories of damages.
steps.prompt: Type the English meaning of this opening line from memory, in a few words.
acceptable: there are four primary categories of damages
there are four primary categories of damage
there are four fathers of damages
steps.feedback: Typing an answer from memory is a stronger test of durable mastery than recognizing it among choices.

steps.title: Categories are not a verdict
steps.translation: To learn · to understand · to ask.
steps.prompt: You can now name and compare the categories of damage. What is Seder's role from here?
answers: Support careful study of the categories and their reasoning while directing any real liability question to qualified guidance.
Provide enough of the categories that a learner could reasonably settle a real damages dispute entirely on their own.
Leave the categories unstudied altogether, since damages law carries real-world consequences for real people.
steps.feedback: Right. Real damages turn on facts, intent, and context far beyond four category names — study the structure, and send the actual case to an authority.

labs.focus: Read a Mishnah by identifying its subject, its scope, and the question hidden inside a general statement.

steps.title: What action is named?
steps.translation: All may slaughter.
steps.prompt: What does the Mishnah state before listing qualifications or exceptions?
answers: A broad statement about who may perform an action.
A narrative set during one of the pilgrimage festivals.
A physical measurement defining the size of a courtyard.
steps.feedback: Good. First locate the scope of the statement — this opens with who may act, not a narrative or a measurement.

steps.title: A general word creates work
steps.translation: All.
steps.prompt: What should a careful Gemara reader ask when seeing “all”?
answers: Who is included, and are there any exceptions?
Which earlier tractate this word was borrowed from?
How many times the word appears across the Mishnah?
steps.feedback: Exactly. A sweeping ‘all’ is an invitation to ask about inclusion and exception, not about word-counts or borrowings.

steps.title: The rule names its own limits
steps.translation: Except a deaf-mute, an imbecile, and a minor.
steps.prompt: The broad ‘all may slaughter’ is immediately narrowed by this exclusion. What does the exception reveal about the rule?
answers: The rule assumes a slaughterer with reliable legal competence — the excluded three are precisely those whose competence is in doubt.
The rule was effectively overturned by its exception, so that in ordinary practice almost no one is actually permitted to slaughter.
The three excluded categories are unique to the laws of slaughter and are found nowhere else across the rest of the Mishnah.
steps.feedback: Good. Reading the exception exposes the rule's hidden assumption — and this exact three-category clause recurs across Shas wherever reliable competence is required.

steps.title: Why competence, not identity
steps.translation: Lest they ruin the slaughter.
steps.prompt: The concern is that these three might ruin the slaughter through unreliable action, not who they are as people. Why does that distinction matter?
answers: It grounds the exclusion in a functional worry about the act's reliability, which can change if reliability can be established.
It shows the exclusion to be a fixed and permanent judgment about the inherent worth of those who are excluded.
It proves that the slaughter counts as invalid only once it has actually been ruined, and never as a precaution beforehand.
steps.feedback: Right. The reason is functional, not personal — the same move you met in the honor-parents chain, where a category's stated reason maps its exact reach.

steps.title: Recall, don't just recognize
steps.translation: All may slaughter.
steps.prompt: Type the English meaning of this opening rule from memory, in a few words.
steps.feedback: Typing an answer from memory is a stronger test of durable mastery than recognizing it among choices.

steps.title: What is this activity for?
steps.translation: To learn · to understand · to ask.
steps.prompt: Slaughter is a live, consequential area of practice. How should a learner treat this source?
answers: Study its structure and reasoning while recognizing that Seder is not issuing a ruling on actual practice.
Treat the Mishnah's rule as sufficient guidance for performing an actual slaughter.
Set the source aside, since a topic with practical stakes cannot be studied safely.
steps.feedback: Right. Source literacy includes knowing the boundary between learning a rule's structure and applying it — the middle path between self-ruling and avoidance.

labs.focus: Approach a sensitive legal tractate through careful textual orientation and the study-aid boundary.

steps.title: Name the subject carefully
steps.translation: All women are presumed to be in a state of purity.
steps.prompt: What kind of opening does the Mishnah provide?
answers: A general presumption that frames later cases.
A direct and personal instruction addressed straight to the individual learner.
A short biblical narrative recounting an account of events that happened in the past.
steps.feedback: Correct. Start by identifying the legal framing without treating it as personal guidance.

steps.title: A presumption is not every case
steps.translation: Presumption / established status.
steps.prompt: What reading habit helps with a statement of presumption?
answers: Ask how the later discussion defines its scope and limits.
Assume it answers every possible question.
Skip the source because it is difficult.
steps.feedback: Exactly. Gemara teaches learners to examine the conditions of a general rule.

steps.title: How a presumption actually works
steps.translation: In the presumed status · until it becomes known otherwise.
steps.prompt: As a reasoning move, what does placing someone 'in a chazakah of purity' accomplish?
answers: It sets a default that holds until specific evidence overturns it, so one reasons forward from an established status rather than from doubt.
It permanently fixes the status in place, so that no later evidence, however clear it may be, could ever change it under any circumstance.
It means that the status is treated as entirely unknown, so that every future case has to be decided instead by a coin toss or by lot.
steps.feedback: Right. A chazakah is a reasoning default: the established state governs until something specific displaces it. This is a general logical tool, not a personal ruling.

steps.title: Recall, don't just recognize
steps.translation: presumption; established status.
steps.prompt: Type the English meaning of חֲזָקָה (chazakah) from memory, in a word or two.
steps.feedback: Typing it from memory beats recognizing it. Chazakah -- a 'presumption', an established status that holds until displaced -- is the reasoning tool this Mishnah opens with.

steps.title: Learn responsibly
steps.translation: Study.
steps.prompt: What is Seder’s role with sensitive halakhic material?
answers: Support careful learning while directing practical questions to qualified guidance.
Replace qualified rabbinic guidance entirely with a single automatic answer from the app itself.
Avoid ever showing the learner the underlying source text itself at all, for any reason.
steps.feedback: Right. Moral seriousness includes making the learning boundary explicit.

labs.focus: Read a Mishnah that assigns different court sizes to different categories of law, and keep the line between study and judicial authority.

steps.title: A court's size depends on the case
steps.translation: Monetary cases are judged by three.
steps.prompt: What does the Mishnah establish before describing any particular case?
answers: That the composition of a court depends on the category of case before it.
That every case in Jewish law requires the same court.
That monetary disputes are decided by a single judge alone.
steps.feedback: Right. A counted opening like this signals a system of court sizes, not one fixed court.

steps.title: The number rises with the stakes
steps.translation: Capital cases are judged by twenty-three.
steps.prompt: What does the jump from three judges to twenty-three suggest about the Mishnah's reasoning?
answers: A higher-stakes case requires a larger court, not just a stricter standard of proof.
The number of judges has nothing to do with the severity of the case.
Capital cases were judged by the same three judges as monetary cases.
steps.feedback: Exactly. Court size itself is a legal safeguard, scaled to consequence.

steps.title: Safeguards scaled to the stakes
steps.translation: Added stringency · according to the matter.
steps.prompt: What general legal instinct does scaling court size to the stakes express?
answers: The graver and less reversible a decision is, the more procedural protection it deserves -- more judges means more deliberation before an irreversible verdict.
That larger and more populous cities were simply entitled to staff their own local courts with a greater number of sitting judges.
That the number of judges was fixed mainly in order to give more young scholars a chance to gain some practical courtroom experience.
steps.feedback: Right. Court size is a scaled safeguard: the weightier and less reversible the outcome, the more judges the law interposes before it -- a principle that generalizes well beyond this case.

steps.title: Recall, don't just recognize
steps.translation: capital cases.
steps.prompt: Type the English meaning of דִּינֵי נְפָשׁוֹת (dinei nefashot) from memory, in a few words.
steps.feedback: Typing it from memory beats recognizing it. Dinei nefashot -- 'capital cases' -- are the highest-stakes cases whose larger court this Mishnah requires.

steps.title: Study is not judicial authority
steps.translation: To learn · to understand · to ask.
steps.prompt: Sanhedrin describes the composition of real courts, including capital courts. What is Seder's role here?
answers: Support careful study of these court structures, while recognizing that real judicial authority belongs to a constituted court and not a course.
Use this particular Mishnah as a basis on which to actually evaluate and decide a real, live legal case today.
Avoid this whole tractate altogether, simply because it happens to discuss the laws of capital punishment.
steps.feedback: Right. Reading how courts were structured is not the same as exercising judicial authority.

labs.focus: Read a procedural requirement by tracing it back to the concern it was designed to solve.

steps.title: A document crosses a distance
steps.translation: One who brings a bill of divorce from a country overseas.
steps.prompt: What situation does the Mishnah introduce before stating any requirement?
answers: A document is being transported a significant distance by an agent.
A court is meeting to judge a monetary dispute.
A wedding is being scheduled for a specific day.
steps.feedback: Good. Locate the situation before asking what extra requirement it triggers.

steps.title: An extra declaration is required
steps.hebrew: צָרִיךְ שֶׁיֹּאמַר בְּפָנַי נִכְתַּב וּבְפָנַי נֶחְתָּם
steps.translation: He must say: it was written in my presence and signed in my presence.
steps.prompt: Why might a document from overseas need this declaration, when a local document does not?
answers: Because the original witnesses cannot be summoned later to confirm the document if a question arises.
Because documents written overseas are presumed forged until proven otherwise.
Because the declaration is a ceremonial formula with no real legal function.
steps.feedback: Right. The declaration substitutes for witnesses who are too far away to be called on later.

steps.title: Rabbah hears a different concern
steps.translation: Because they are not expert in [writing it] for her sake.
steps.prompt: Rabbah gives another reason for the declaration: a get must be written for this specific woman, and distant communities may not know that law. What kind of reason is this?
answers: A concern about how the document was created, where Rava's concern was about proving it authentic later.
A concern that overseas scribes write the document in a language the court cannot read.
A stricter version of Rava's concern, extending witness-verification back to the writing itself.
steps.feedback: Good. Rabbah worries about lishmah — the writing's intention; Rava about later authentication. Same requirement, two genuinely different failure modes.

steps.title: The dispute is about the why
steps.translation: Rabbah · Rava.
steps.prompt: Rabbah and Rava agree completely on the requirement itself — the agent must make the declaration. What does a machloket about reasons, rather than rules, produce?
answers: Different outcomes at the edges: cases where one concern applies and the other does not will test which reason governs.
A rule that remains suspended and unenforceable until the two reasons are reconciled.
A free choice for later courts to adopt whichever of the two reasons persuades them.
steps.feedback: Exactly. The Gemara itself chases the edge cases — and later concludes that Rabbah accepts Rava's concern too, adding his own on top. Reasons have consequences; that is why the sugya bothers.

steps.title: From remedy to risk
steps.translation: Enactment · concern.
steps.prompt: This lab's whole method has been to read a procedural requirement backward to the concern it answers. Why is that a transferable Gemara skill?
answers: Because rabbinic enactments are engineered around specific failure modes — naming the risk explains the remedy's exact shape and limits.
Because every requirement in the Talmud responds to a documented historical incident.
Because a requirement whose governing reason is unknown loses its force and may be set aside by later courts.
steps.feedback: Right. Reading remedy-to-risk explains why THIS declaration, for THESE documents, from THESE distances — and the same reading move opens enactments across Shas.

steps.title: Recall, don't just recognize
steps.translation: It was written in my presence and signed in my presence.
steps.prompt: This is the declaration the whole sugya turns on. Type its English meaning from memory.
acceptable: it was written in my presence and signed in my presence
in my presence it was written and in my presence it was signed
it was written before me and signed before me
written in my presence and signed in my presence
steps.feedback: Typing an answer from memory is a stronger test of durable mastery than recognizing it among choices.

steps.title: Study is not practical guidance
steps.translation: To learn · to understand · to ask.
steps.prompt: Gittin addresses real divorce documents with real consequences for a person's status. What is Seder's role here?
answers: Support careful study of the procedure and its reasoning while directing any real situation to a qualified rabbinic authority.
Use this Mishnah as a checklist for evaluating a real document's validity.
Avoid studying the tractate altogether because divorce is a sensitive subject.
steps.feedback: Right. A procedure this consequential can be studied seriously without standing in for qualified guidance.

labs.focus: Notice a legal asymmetry the Mishnah states without comment, and ask what it reveals.

steps.title: A counted list opens the tractate
steps.translation: A woman is acquired [in marriage] in three ways.
steps.prompt: What kind of statement opens this tractate?
answers: A counted list of the valid ways a marriage can be formed.
A single fixed procedure that admits of no alternatives.
A narrative about one specific couple and their wedding.
steps.feedback: Good. A counted opening signals a system of valid methods, not one fixed procedure.

steps.title: Entry and exit are not symmetric
steps.translation: And she acquires herself [is released] in two ways.
steps.prompt: What does the shift from three ways to two ways invite a careful reader to ask?
answers: Why entry into the legal status and exit from it are not structured identically.
Whether the Mishnah has simply made an arithmetical slip in its counting.
Whether marriage and release are exactly the same process in reverse.
steps.feedback: Exactly. Noticing an asymmetry the text states matter-of-factly is a real close-reading skill.

steps.title: The three ways are named
steps.translation: By money, by document, and by intercourse.
steps.prompt: The Mishnah names the three valid mechanisms. What work does a list of legal mechanisms do?
answers: It defines which acts create the status — anything outside the list, whatever its sincerity, does not effect it.
It ranks the three mechanisms from the most honorable way to marry down to the least.
It records the three customs that were most widespread when the Mishnah was compiled.
steps.feedback: Good. This is a closed legal list, not a ranking and not ethnography — the Gemara will ask where each mechanism comes from, starting with money.

steps.title: The two exits are named
steps.translation: By a bill of divorce and by the husband's death.
steps.prompt: Entry has three mechanisms; exit has two, and they are entirely different acts. What does the full comparison show?
answers: The status is created and dissolved by different legal instruments — the asymmetry is structural, not an oversight.
Exit from the status was deliberately designed to be procedurally easier than entry into it.
The two lists must once have matched, and one mechanism has been lost from the exit list.
steps.feedback: Exactly. Money, document, and intercourse create; only a get or death dissolves. Mapping both lists precisely is what lets the tractate's later chapters make sense.

steps.title: Acquired here, consecrated later
steps.translation: A woman is acquired · a man betroths [consecrates].
steps.prompt: Chapter one opens in the passive language of acquisition; chapter two opens with the man actively being makdesh — consecrating. The Gemara itself discusses this word choice. What should a reader do with it?
answers: Treat the shift as data: the Mishnah speaks Torah's acquisition-language first, then the sages' consecration-language, and each frames the institution differently.
Conclude that the two chapters were written by different authors with different views of marriage.
Read it as ordinary stylistic variation, since legal writers avoid repeating the same word too often.
steps.feedback: Right. Kinyan-language ties the law to its biblical sources; kiddushin-language — setting apart, as something consecrated — is the sages' own frame. The Gemara weighs both words deliberately.

steps.title: Where does money come from?
steps.translation: "Taking" [learned from] "taking" at the field of Ephron.
steps.prompt: The Gemara derives money-betrothal by linking the Torah's "when a man takes a wife" to Abraham "taking" Ephron's field for silver — a gezeira shava between two uses of one word. What is this derivation doing?
answers: Grounding a mechanism in Torah through a formal verbal analogy — one of the tradition's named reasoning tools, not a loose association.
Proving that betrothal is legally identical in every respect to purchasing land from a seller.
Showing that the Torah requires silver specifically for a valid betrothal.
steps.feedback: Good. A gezeira shava transfers a defined legal point through shared language — here, that "taking" can be effected by money. It does not equate a wife with a field, and the Gemara elsewhere makes that difference explicit.

steps.title: Recall, don't just recognize
steps.translation: A woman is acquired [in marriage] in three ways.
steps.prompt: You have worked this opening line from several angles. Type its English meaning from memory, in a few words.
acceptable: a woman is acquired in three ways
the woman is acquired in three ways
a woman is acquired by three ways
a woman is acquired through three ways
a woman is acquired in marriage in three ways
steps.feedback: Typing an answer from memory is a stronger test of durable mastery than recognizing it among choices.

steps.title: Study is not a personal ruling
steps.translation: To learn · to understand · to ask.
steps.prompt: Kiddushin addresses real marital status with real consequences. What is Seder's role here?
answers: Support careful study of the structure and reasoning while directing any real situation to a qualified rabbinic authority.
Use this Mishnah as the basis for resolving a real personal-status question.
Avoid studying the tractate altogether because marriage is a sensitive subject.
steps.feedback: Right. Structural literacy about a legal status is not the same as ruling on someone's actual status.

labs.focus: Read a Mishnah about shared property by tracking whose obligation follows from a shared request.

steps.title: Co-owners want to divide space
steps.translation: Partners who wished to make a partition in a courtyard.
steps.prompt: What situation does the Mishnah place before the reader?
answers: Co-owners of a shared space who want to divide it between them.
A single owner deciding on his own what to build on his land.
A court adjudicating a dispute over an alleged act of theft.
steps.feedback: Right. A shared-property case starts with the parties and their shared stake, before any ruling.

steps.title: Where the wall is built matters
steps.translation: They build the wall in the middle.
steps.prompt: What does building the wall in the middle, rather than on one owner's side, suggest about the underlying principle?
answers: A cost or obligation shared equally between co-owners should be reflected in the physical result, not favor one side.
The finished wall belongs entirely to whichever of the partners first requested that it be built.
The precise location of the wall within the courtyard carries no legal significance whatsoever.
steps.feedback: Exactly. A physical detail like placement can encode a legal principle about shared obligation.

steps.title: Why must there be a wall at all?
steps.translation: Damage of sight is called damage.
steps.prompt: The Gemara asks what obligates a partition in the first place, and reaches a startling idea: being seen in one's own space can itself be a legal harm. What makes this claim significant?
answers: It treats loss of privacy — being watched — as a real injury, not merely an annoyance a neighbor must tolerate.
It rules that any neighbor may look freely into an adjoining courtyard whenever they wish.
It shows that only physical damage to property can ever count as legal harm.
steps.feedback: Good. Whether hezek re'iyah is ‘damage’ is one of the tractate's opening disputes — the answer decides whether privacy is a right the law will enforce.

steps.title: How high, and why that height
steps.translation: Four cubits.
steps.prompt: The wall must reach four cubits — higher than an average person. Why does the law fix that specific height?
answers: Because a wall taller than a person blocks the sightline, so the measure is engineered to solve the exact privacy concern.
Because four cubits is a round number the sages preferred for all construction.
Because the height marks ownership rather than serving any practical function.
steps.feedback: Exactly. The measure is not arbitrary — it is the height that actually defeats hezek re'iyah, the concern the previous step named.

steps.title: Keep the structure visible
steps.translation: Partnership · request · obligation.
steps.prompt: Which sequence describes the structure you just traced?
answers: A shared arrangement, one partner's request, and the obligation that follows for both.
A ranking of the two partners according to who owns the larger share of the courtyard.
A dispute that the Mishnah records here without ever resolving which partner must build.
steps.feedback: Good. Naming the sequence -- arrangement, request, obligation -- is a skill that transfers to other shared-property sugyot.

steps.title: Recall, don't just recognize
steps.translation: They build the wall in the middle.
steps.prompt: Type the English meaning of this ruling from memory, in a few words.
acceptable: they build the wall in the middle
they build the wall in the center
the wall is built in the middle
build the wall in the middle
steps.feedback: Typing an answer from memory is a stronger test of durable mastery than recognizing it among choices.

labs.focus: Read a counted Mishnah that opens with fifteen categories before any single case is explained.

steps.title: Fifteen categories, named at once
steps.translation: Fifteen women exempt their rival wives.
steps.prompt: What does opening with a specific number of categories signal about the coming discussion?
answers: A defined, closed list that the Mishnah will work through case by case.
An open-ended topic with no fixed boundary on how many cases it holds.
A single narrative about one particular family and its circumstances.
steps.feedback: Right. A precise count promises a complete, enumerable list, not a loose collection of examples.

steps.title: What does 'exempt' do here?
steps.translation: Exempt from chalitzah and from levirate marriage.
steps.prompt: What kind of legal move does 'exempt' describe here?
answers: One woman's forbidden status can release a second, otherwise-obligated woman from an obligation tied to the same marriage.
The word here means the opposite of what it seems: it creates a new obligation rather than removing an existing one.
It carries no real technical meaning in this Mishnah and is used only as a loose figure of speech.
steps.feedback: Exactly. Tracking exactly what a technical term releases, and for whom, is the core skill this tractate demands.

steps.title: A forbidden relation exempts her co-wife
steps.translation: The rival wife of a forbidden relation.
steps.prompt: The fifteen women are all arayot — relations a man may not marry (his daughter among them). When such a woman is a widow awaiting levirate marriage, she is exempt, and so is her co-wife (tzara). Why does one woman's status release the other?
answers: Yibum lifts only the prohibition on a brother's widow, not a deeper forbidden relation, so an ervah and her co-wife both drop out.
Because the two co-wives are treated as legally interchangeable, so whatever applies to one of them applies automatically to the other.
Because the court prefers, as a general policy, to exempt more women than fewer whenever the facts of a case are left in doubt.
steps.feedback: Right. Yibum lifts one specific prohibition, not every forbidden relation — so an ervah is never drawn in, and her tzara is freed along with her. This tzarat-ervah principle is the whole chapter's engine.

steps.title: Recall, don't just recognize
steps.translation: Fifteen women exempt their rival wives.
steps.prompt: Type the English meaning of this opening line from memory, in a few words.
acceptable: fifteen women exempt their rival wives
fifteen women free their rival wives
fifteen women exempt their fellow wives
steps.feedback: Typing an answer from memory is a stronger test of durable mastery than recognizing it among choices.

steps.title: Study is not a personal ruling
steps.translation: To learn · to understand · to ask.
steps.prompt: Yevamot addresses complex, real family-status law. What is Seder's role here?
answers: Support careful study of the structure and reasoning while directing any real situation to a qualified rabbinic authority.
Use this Mishnah directly to resolve a real family-status question that has arisen in one's own life.
Avoid studying the tractate at all, on the grounds that family-status law is too sensitive a subject.
steps.feedback: Right. This tractate rewards careful study precisely because its real cases need qualified guidance, not a course.

labs.focus: Read a Mishnah about ancient polytheistic practice as historical and legal literacy, not commentary on any living faith.

steps.title: A rule defined by a window of time
steps.hebrew: לִפְנֵי אֵידֵיהֶן שֶׁל עוֹבְדֵי כּוֹכָבִים שְׁלֹשָׁה יָמִים
steps.translation: Before the festivals of idol-worshippers, for three days.
steps.prompt: What kind of rule does the Mishnah build here?
answers: A rule defined by a window of time before a specific public event, not a permanent restriction.
A rule with no time limit at all, restricting the same conduct on every day of the year alike.
A description of how the idol-worshippers' own festivals were observed and celebrated.
steps.feedback: Right. This is a temporal boundary, not a blanket prohibition -- notice exactly what it does and does not cover.

steps.title: What the prohibition guards against
steps.translation: It is forbidden to conduct business with them.
steps.prompt: The Gemara explains this concern as: profitable trade just before a festival could lead a trading partner to credit their success to their god. What kind of concern is this?
answers: A concern about inadvertently facilitating someone else's act of religious thanksgiving, not a judgment about the person themselves.
A concern about the fair market price at which the goods in the transaction are being bought and sold.
A concern about commerce in general that has no particular connection to the timing of any festival at all.
steps.feedback: Right. The Mishnah's concern is about avoiding facilitation of a specific ritual act, in a specific ancient context.

steps.title: A tractate of law opens with a drama
steps.hebrew: עָתִיד הַקָּדוֹשׁ בָּרוּךְ הוּא לְהָבִיא סֵפֶר תּוֹרָה
steps.translation: In the future the Holy One will bring a Torah scroll [and say: whoever engaged with this, come collect their reward].
steps.prompt: Rather than analyze the Mishnah first, the Gemara opens with an end-of-days scene: God offers reward for Torah, and the nations come to claim it. Why open a legal tractate this way?
answers: The aggadah frames the whole subject — before ruling on relations with idolatry, the Gemara stages the deepest question of reward, obligation, and who kept the covenant.
The passage is simply misplaced, and by its content really belongs in a tractate devoted to the world to come and final judgment.
The scene is a light narrative introduction included for interest, with no real bearing on how the tractate goes on to reason.
steps.feedback: Good. A halakhic tractate can open in the register of aggadah — the drama sets the moral stakes the dry rules will then work out.

steps.title: What Rome answers
steps.translation: We established marketplaces, we built bathhouses.
steps.prompt: Asked what they accomplished, Rome answers that it built markets and bathhouses — ‘all for the sake of Israel, so they could study Torah.’ What is the Gemara doing with this reply?
answers: Letting the empire's self-justification be voiced, then tested — the aggadah examines motive, not just achievement.
Endorsing Rome's claim that its public works were genuinely done to benefit Torah study.
Recording a neutral list of Roman construction projects with no argument attached.
steps.feedback: Right. The scene puts the claim in Rome's own mouth precisely so the sugya can weigh whether deeds done for one's own benefit earn a covenant's reward.

steps.title: Read this as historical literacy
steps.translation: A time period · a reason · a boundary.
steps.prompt: What historical-literacy habit does this sugya call for?
answers: Read the rule as addressed to a specific ancient religious context, and ask what concern it was solving, rather than applying its categories directly to any community today.
Apply the rule automatically and directly to any religious community one happens to encounter in the present day, whatever its actual beliefs.
Set the tractate aside entirely and refuse to study it, on the assumption that ancient legal categories can never repay careful reading.
steps.feedback: Right. Careful historical reading means naming exactly what concern a rule addressed in its own setting.

steps.title: Recall, don't just recognize
steps.translation: Before their festivals, three days.
steps.prompt: Type the English meaning of this opening time-window from memory, in a few words.
acceptable: for three days before their festivals
before their festivals for three days
steps.feedback: Typing an answer from memory is a stronger test of durable mastery than recognizing it among choices.

labs.focus: Read a Mishnah that describes an extended preparation period, then ask what risk that preparation is designed to prevent.

steps.title: A fixed preparation period
steps.hebrew: שִׁבְעַת יָמִים קֹדֶם יוֹם הַכִּפּוּרִים מַפְרִישִׁין כֹּהֵן גָּדוֹל
steps.translation: Seven days before Yom Kippur, the High Priest is separated [from his house].
steps.prompt: What does the Mishnah establish before describing what happens during those seven days?
answers: A fixed preparation period before a single, non-repeatable annual service.
A one-time ruling that established no ongoing yearly practice at all.
A description of an ordinary priestly duty performed on any weekday.
steps.feedback: Right. Notice the scale of the preparation before asking why it is needed.

steps.title: What the separation guards against
steps.translation: Lest a disqualification occur to him.
steps.prompt: What kind of concern does this phrase reveal about the seven-day separation?
answers: A concern that an unpredictable event could make the one prepared person unable to serve, with no way to substitute mid-process.
A concern about safeguarding the High Priest's personal wealth during the days he is kept apart from his household.
A concern about ritual detail that has nothing to do with whether the Yom Kippur service can actually be performed.
steps.feedback: Exactly. A long lead time exists to manage a risk that could not be fixed at the last moment.

steps.title: Where do seven days come from?
steps.hebrew: כַּאֲשֶׁר עָשָׂה בַּיּוֹם הַזֶּה צִוָּה ה׳ לַעֲשׂוֹת
steps.translation: As was done this day, the Lord commanded to do.
steps.prompt: The Gemara derives the seven days from the seven-day inauguration of the priests (Leviticus 8), reading ‘to do’ as covering both the red heifer and Yom Kippur. What kind of reasoning is this?
answers: Anchoring a later practice in a Torah verse by reading one phrase as instructing several distinct preparations.
Inventing an entirely new requirement that the Torah itself never connects to the priesthood in any way.
Recording a much later custom that arose after the Temple and was then read back into the verse retroactively.
steps.feedback: Good. The milu'im — the seven days that ‘filled’ the priests into their role — become the model for every seven-day priestly separation.

steps.title: Preparing for the risk
steps.translation: And they prepare another priest in his place.
steps.prompt: The Mishnah provides that a second priest is readied in case the first becomes disqualified. How does this complete the structure the reason opened?
answers: The named risk — a last-minute disqualification — is answered by a standby who has also been prepared, so the service can never fail for lack of a priest.
The backup priest replaces the first one permanently, since the law in fact appoints two High Priests every single year.
The backup exists only as a matter of honor, and by law could never actually step in to perform the service himself.
steps.feedback: Exactly. Concern and backup fit together: an irreplaceable service is protected by preparing a replacement in advance.

steps.title: Keep the structure visible
steps.translation: Separation · concern · substitute.
steps.prompt: Which sequence describes the structure you just traced?
answers: An extended preparation period, a named risk it guards against, and a backup put in place for that risk.
A ranking of priests from most to least qualified for the service.
A dispute over whether the seven-day separation is required at all.
steps.feedback: Good. This risk-and-backup structure recurs anywhere a single, non-repeatable service is at stake.

steps.title: Recall, don't just recognize
steps.translation: Lest a disqualification occur to him.
steps.prompt: Type the English meaning of the phrase that names the whole structure's concern, in a few words.
acceptable: lest a disqualification occur to him
lest a disqualification happen to him
in case a disqualification occurs to him
lest some disqualification occur to him
steps.feedback: Typing an answer from memory is a stronger test of durable mastery than recognizing it among choices.

labs.focus: Read a Mishnah that names multiple new years, each for a different legal purpose.

steps.title: Four new years, not one
steps.translation: There are four new years.
steps.prompt: What does opening with this count suggest about the concept of a 'year' in this Mishnah?
answers: That 'year' is not one fixed concept, but depends on what is being counted or dated.
That the calendar has exactly one new year and the rest are errors.
That the precise number of new years carries no real legal significance.
steps.feedback: Right. A single word like 'year' can quietly cover several distinct legal counting systems.

steps.title: Each date solves a different problem
steps.hebrew: בְּאֶחָד בְּנִיסָן רֹאשׁ הַשָּׁנָה לַמְּלָכִים וְלָרְגָלִים
steps.translation: On the first of Nisan is the new year for kings and for festivals.
steps.prompt: What does pairing a specific date with a specific legal purpose accomplish?
answers: It shows each new year exists to solve a distinct counting problem, such as dating a king's reign or sequencing the festivals.
It shows that Nisan is the only date that truly matters anywhere in the entire Mishnah.
It proves that kings and festivals share no meaningful relationship to calendar dates at all.
steps.feedback: Exactly. Different legal questions can require different calendars, even within the same tradition.

steps.title: Keep the structure visible
steps.translation: A count · a date · a purpose.
steps.prompt: What reading habit does a multi-purpose calendar Mishnah like this reward?
answers: Ask which specific legal purpose each date is solving, rather than assuming 'new year' means one single thing.
Assume every date in the Mishnah ultimately refers to one and the same purpose.
Skip over the specific dates, since only the total count of four carries meaning.
steps.feedback: Good. This habit -- match each detail to the specific purpose it serves -- carries into any Mishnah that counts categories.

steps.title: Tishrei's own new year
steps.hebrew: בְּאֶחָד בְּתִשְׁרֵי רֹאשׁ הַשָּׁנָה לַשָּׁנִים וְלַשְּׁמִיטִּין וְלַיּוֹבְלוֹת
steps.translation: On the first of Tishrei is the new year for years, for sabbatical cycles, and for jubilees.
steps.prompt: The Tishrei date — the Rosh Hashanah of the liturgical calendar — carries the counting of years, shemitah, and yovel. What does seeing it as one of four teach?
answers: Even the most familiar new year is one purpose-built calendar among several, each serving its own legal count.
The Tishrei new year outranks the other three, which exist only as technicalities.
The four dates were once a single new year that later generations divided.
steps.feedback: Right. The Mishnah's structure resists the assumption that our most familiar date is the only real one — each of the four is real for what it counts.

steps.title: The trees get two opinions
steps.hebrew: בֵּית שַׁמַּאי אוֹמְרִים בְּאֶחָד בִּשְׁבָט · בֵּית הִלֵּל אוֹמְרִים בַּחֲמִשָּׁה עָשָׂר בּוֹ
steps.translation: Beit Shammai say: on the first of Shevat. Beit Hillel say: on the fifteenth of it.
steps.prompt: The new year for trees arrives with a Shammai–Hillel dispute inside the Mishnah itself. What should a reader who knows this pair already do?
answers: Recognize the recurring disputants, expect the halakha to follow Hillel, and still ask what reasoning distinguishes the two dates here.
Skip the dispute, since its outcome is already known from every other Shammai–Hillel case.
Treat the dispute as evidence that the tree new year was never actually observed in practice.
steps.feedback: Exactly. Tu BiShvat is Beit Hillel's fifteenth — the recurring pair reaches even into the calendar, and informed expectation still leaves the reasoning worth reading.

steps.title: Why a ram's horn
steps.hebrew: תִּקְעוּ לְפָנַי בְּשׁוֹפָר שֶׁל אַיִל כְּדֵי שֶׁאֶזְכּוֹר לָכֶם עֲקֵידַת יִצְחָק
steps.translation: Sound before Me a shofar of a ram, so that I will remember for you the binding of Isaac.
steps.prompt: Later in the tractate, the Gemara gives the ram's horn its meaning: the binding of Isaac, carried into ritual memory. What kind of connection is this?
answers: A narrative from Genesis becoming the stated meaning of the tractate's own central ritual — story and practice joined in one source.
A ruling that only a ram's horn is valid because rams were commonly available in the Temple era.
An aside about the Akeidah with no bearing on how the tractate understands the shofar.
steps.feedback: Right. If you came here from the Akeidah unit, this is the sugya it promised — the story you close-read is the memory this tractate's shofar carries.

steps.title: Recall, don't just recognize
steps.translation: There are four new years.
steps.prompt: Type the English meaning of this opening line from memory, in a few words.
acceptable: there are four heads of years
there are four heads of the year
steps.feedback: Typing an answer from memory is a stronger test of durable mastery than recognizing it among choices.

labs.focus: Read a liturgical-timing dispute by tracing the symbolic reasoning behind each side.

steps.title: A timing question opens the tractate
steps.translation: From when do we mention the power of rain [in prayer]?
steps.prompt: What kind of question opens this tractate?
answers: A timing question about when a specific line enters the standing prayer.
A meteorological question about how much rain actually fell in a given year.
A settled ruling stated on its own, with no underlying question behind it.
steps.feedback: Right. The tractate opens mid-question, not mid-ruling -- expect a dispute to follow.

steps.title: A reason behind the timing
steps.translation: Because rain during the festival [of Sukkot] is a sign of a curse.
steps.prompt: What reasoning does this position give for delaying the mention of rain?
answers: Praying for rain during a festival when people dwell outdoors would work against the festival's own purpose.
Rain is never mentioned anywhere in the fixed language of Jewish prayer, in any season of the year.
The timing of the festival has no bearing whatsoever on the content of the prayers said around it.
steps.feedback: Right. A position about 'when' often rests on a substantive concern, not an arbitrary date.

steps.title: Rain named among the powers of God
steps.translation: We mention the power of rain in [the blessing of] the resurrection of the dead.
steps.prompt: The line about rain is inserted into the Amidah's blessing that ends with the resurrection of the dead. Why is rain placed there, and called a ‘mighty act’?
answers: Because rain revives the parched earth as God revives the dead — both are powers of giving life, so they share a blessing.
Because the blessing had an empty space that the sages filled with an unrelated seasonal line.
Because rain, unlike resurrection, is an ordinary event that needed elevating by association.
steps.feedback: Good. The placement is an argument: controlling life-giving rain sits beside raising the dead as one divine power — the liturgy's structure carries the theology.

steps.title: Keep the structure visible
steps.translation: A time · a reason · a sign.
steps.prompt: What does tracing this reasoning teach about reading a timing dispute?
answers: A position about 'when' often connects a date to a substantive symbolic or practical concern, not an arbitrary choice.
Timing disputes in the Mishnah are always arbitrary and carry no underlying reasoning.
Only the final accepted position is worth reading, so the reasoning behind it can be skipped.
steps.feedback: Good. Timing disputes reward the same discipline as any other machloket: trace the reason, not just the ruling.

steps.title: Recall, don't just recognize
steps.translation: The power of rain.
steps.prompt: Type the English meaning of this phrase — the tractate's name for the rain-line in prayer — from memory.
steps.feedback: Typing an answer from memory is a stronger test of durable mastery than recognizing it among choices.

labs.focus: Read a calendar Mishnah that widens a fixed date into a range, then ask what practical concern justifies the widening.

steps.title: Five days, not one
steps.hebrew: מְגִלָּה נִקְרֵאת בְּאַחַד עָשָׂר בִּשְׁנֵים עָשָׂר בִּשְׁלֹשָׁה עָשָׂר בְּאַרְבָּעָה עָשָׂר וּבַחֲמִשָּׁה עָשָׂר
steps.translation: The Megillah is read on the eleventh, twelfth, thirteenth, fourteenth, or fifteenth.
steps.prompt: What does opening with a five-day range, rather than one fixed date, suggest?
answers: That the obligation is anchored to a specific date but built with flexibility for some communities.
That the exact day of reading never mattered to the Mishnah.
That five unrelated holidays are being listed together in a single opening line.
steps.feedback: Right. A range at the very opening signals a real accommodation built into the law, not an oversight.

steps.title: Why villages could read early
steps.hebrew: כְּדֵי שֶׁיָּסוּפְּקוּ מַיִם וּמָזוֹן לַאֲחֵיהֶם שֶׁבַּכְּרַכִּין
steps.translation: So that they [villagers] could supply water and food to their brothers in the walled cities.
steps.prompt: What practical concern does this reason reveal about the early-reading allowance?
answers: Villagers needed to read on their existing market days so they could still support the larger cities' observance without a scheduling conflict.
Villagers were being penalized with an earlier reading because their observance mattered less than the cities' own.
The stated reason has nothing to do with logistics or with communities supporting one another's observance.
steps.feedback: Right. The flexibility exists to fit the law around real logistics, not to weaken the obligation.

steps.title: A familiar habit, transferred
steps.translation: A date · market days · a need.
steps.prompt: You already learned that Ketubot's wedding schedule was built around fixed court days. What does that habit add here?
answers: A ritual date can be intentionally aligned with an existing practical schedule -- like market days -- rather than set in isolation from ordinary life.
Court days and market days are unique to these two cases and never influenced any other area of Jewish law.
Once one calendar-based reason has been learned, no other date anywhere in Shas needs its own investigation.
steps.feedback: Exactly. The same habit -- ask what ordinary-life schedule a ritual date is built around -- reads Ketubot's Wednesday and Megillah's market days alike.

steps.title: An anchor older than the miracle
steps.hebrew: כְּרַכִּין הַמּוּקָּפִין חוֹמָה מִימוֹת יְהוֹשֻׁעַ בִּן נוּן קוֹרִין בַּחֲמִשָּׁה עָשָׂר
steps.translation: Cities surrounded by a wall from the days of Joshua son of Nun read on the fifteenth.
steps.prompt: The Purim story happened in Persia, yet the walled-city rule is anchored to Joshua's era — a thousand years earlier. What should a careful reader do with that surprising anchor?
answers: Ask why the law chose this anchor — the traditional answer honors the Land of Israel, whose ancient cities lay ruined in Esther's day.
Conclude that the rule originally applied only to those cities that Joshua himself personally conquered.
Treat the anchor as a scribal error for the days of Achashverosh, matching the story's own era.
steps.feedback: Good. A dating anchor is a choice, and this one quietly redraws the holiday's map around the Land of Israel — reading the anchor is reading the law's values.

steps.title: Shushan's own day
steps.translation: And they rested on the fifteenth of it.
steps.prompt: Walled cities read on the fifteenth because the Jews of Shushan rested from their enemies a day later than everyone else. What does this show about the calendar rule?
answers: The law encodes the story's own timeline — the two Purim dates preserve the two days on which relief actually arrived.
The fifteenth was chosen arbitrarily to distinguish city-dwellers from villagers.
Shushan's Jews observed a private holiday that the rest of the people never adopted.
steps.feedback: Exactly. Esther 9's own verses carry the two dates; the Mishnah's calendar is narrative made law.

steps.title: The tractate that retires sacred objects
steps.translation: A worn Torah scroll is stored away.
steps.prompt: Megillah later governs the sale of synagogues and the retirement of worn sacred texts — the practice that created the Cairo Geniza's archive. What does this range teach about tractates?
answers: A tractate gathers a topic's whole lifecycle — from when a scroll is read to what becomes of it when it can no longer be read.
The genizah rule applies only to scrolls of Esther and never to any other kind of sacred text.
The tractate's later chapters simply abandoned its calendar theme in favor of unrelated material.
steps.feedback: Right. If you came here from the Geniza unit, this is the rule that filled the Ben Ezra storeroom — met now in its own tractate.

steps.title: Recall, don't just recognize
steps.translation: Cities surrounded by a wall.
steps.prompt: Type the English meaning of this phrase from memory, in a few words.
steps.feedback: Typing an answer from memory is a stronger test of durable mastery than recognizing it among choices.

labs.focus: Read a Tannaitic dispute by naming the legal category both sides are actually arguing about.

steps.title: A dispute over something new
steps.translation: An egg that was laid on a festival day.
steps.prompt: What situation does the Mishnah open with?
answers: An object that came into existence during the festival itself, not before it.
An object that already existed in full before the festival day had begun.
A narrative passage carrying no real legal content of its own.
steps.feedback: Right. The timing of the egg's existence, not the egg itself, is what the whole dispute turns on.

steps.title: Same case, opposite rulings
steps.hebrew: בֵּית שַׁמַּאי אוֹמְרִים תֵּאָכֵל וּבֵית הִלֵּל אוֹמְרִים לֹא תֵאָכֵל
steps.translation: Beit Shammai say: it may be eaten. Beit Hillel say: it may not be eaten.
steps.prompt: What does this immediate disagreement signal about the underlying legal question?
answers: Something about the egg's status is genuinely unsettled -- whether a thing that first came into being during the festival counts as usable.
One of the two positions recorded here must simply be a later copyist's transcription error rather than a genuine held view.
The two schools here actually agree with each other, and the whole difference between them is only a matter of loose wording.
steps.feedback: Exactly. The concept at stake is "nolad" -- something newly come into being -- and whether that status is treated like ordinary, already-prepared property.

steps.title: Keep the structure visible
steps.translation: Newly come into being.
steps.prompt: What reading habit does a dispute like this reward?
answers: Look past the specific case to name the legal category or concept both sides are actually disagreeing about.
Assume that whichever side states its position in more words is the one that is correct.
Treat the case as too small and trivial to carry any real legal weight worth studying.
steps.feedback: Good. A single Hebrew term can carry an entire legal category once you know what it names.

steps.title: Why does Beit Hillel forbid?
steps.translation: Because of preparation · because of a newly-created thing.
steps.prompt: The Gemara offers two different reasons for Beit Hillel's prohibition: Rabbah says the egg was ‘prepared’ on a preceding Shabbat for the festival; Rav Nachman says it is nolad, a newly-created object set aside like muktzeh. Why does the Gemara pursue two reasons for one agreed ruling?
answers: Because the reason a rule rests on decides how far it reaches — the two reasons apply to different festival-and-Shabbat arrangements, each tested against further cases.
Because the two amoraim are really just restating Beit Hillel's one single reason in two different but interchangeable ways.
Because a ruling can only be relied upon once at least two fully independent reasons have been found to support it.
steps.feedback: Good. A machloket about the reason, not the ruling — you met the same move in Gittin. Which reason governs changes which further cases the prohibition catches.

steps.title: Recall, don't just recognize
steps.translation: An egg that was laid on a festival day.
steps.prompt: Type the English meaning of this opening case from memory, in a few words.
acceptable: an egg that was laid on a festival day
an egg laid on a festival day
an egg that was laid on yom tov
an egg laid on yom tov
an egg born on a festival day
steps.feedback: Typing an answer from memory is a stronger test of durable mastery than recognizing it among choices.

labs.focus: Read a permitted-labor Mishnah by tracing the concern it protects against.

steps.title: Ordinary labor, an unusual day
steps.translation: One may water a field that requires irrigation during the intermediate festival days.
steps.prompt: What kind of activity does the Mishnah address first?
answers: A form of labor ordinarily restricted during the intermediate festival days, now explicitly permitted.
An activity that is only ever permitted outside of any festival period, at ordinary times of the year.
A purely symbolic ritual act that serves no practical agricultural function at all.
steps.feedback: Right. Chol HaMoed limits ordinary labor -- so an explicit permission here is doing real legal work.

steps.title: What justifies the exception
steps.translation: A matter that would be lost.
steps.prompt: What kind of concern lets ordinarily-restricted labor become permitted here?
answers: Preventing a real, otherwise-unavoidable financial loss the delay of the festival would cause.
A general dislike of having to rest from productive labor during the intermediate days.
A separate area of law that is entirely unrelated to the festival and its restrictions.
steps.feedback: Exactly. "Prevention of loss" is a recognized category that reopens what the festival's rest would otherwise restrict.

steps.title: Keep the structure visible
steps.translation: Prohibition · permission · reason.
steps.prompt: What does tracing a permitted exception like this teach about reading festival law?
answers: A default restriction and its exception both deserve equal attention -- the exception often reveals the restriction's real purpose.
Exceptions are only rare departures from the real law and are therefore not worth reading closely.
Once a general restriction has been stated, no genuinely permitted case could ever exist alongside it.
steps.feedback: Good. Reading the exception carefully is often the fastest way to understand what the underlying restriction was protecting.

steps.title: Even loss-prevention has a ceiling
steps.translation: Excessive exertion.
steps.prompt: Loss-prevention permits the labor — but only if it does not require excessive exertion (watering from a spring is allowed; hauling buckets is not). Why cap a permission meant to prevent loss?
answers: Because the whole point is to protect the festival's rest and joy; heavy toil would damage that spirit more than the worry over loss would.
Because excessive exertion is a separate prohibition that has nothing to do with the festival at all.
Because the sages doubted that heavy labor could ever actually prevent a real financial loss.
steps.feedback: Right. The exception serves the rule it bends: loss-prevention is allowed to preserve the festival's ease, so labor that destroys that ease is exactly what the cap excludes.

steps.title: Recall, don't just recognize
steps.translation: A matter that would be lost.
steps.prompt: Type the English meaning of this category — the reason the labor is permitted — from memory.
acceptable: a matter that would be lost
a thing that would be lost
a matter that would be lost
steps.feedback: Typing an answer from memory is a stronger test of durable mastery than recognizing it among choices.

labs.focus: Recognize a recurring Mishnaic structure -- a broad obligation immediately narrowed by a named exception.

steps.title: A broad obligation opens the tractate
steps.translation: All are obligated in the appearance-offering.
steps.prompt: What kind of statement opens this tractate?
answers: A sweeping obligation, stated before any exception.
A single ruling limited to one specific person.
A description with no legal content.
steps.feedback: Good. First locate the scope of the obligation before its exceptions narrow it.

steps.title: A familiar exception clause
steps.translation: Except a deaf-mute, an imbecile, and a minor.
steps.prompt: You have read this exact exception clause before, in Chullin. What does its reappearance here suggest?
answers: This three-category exclusion is a recurring Mishnaic pattern, applied across different areas of law wherever reliable legal competence is required.
This particular phrase only ever appears in the specific context of the laws of ritual slaughter, and nowhere else at all.
Its reappearance here is really just a coincidence, one that carries no shared underlying logic between the two places.
steps.feedback: Exactly. The same exception clause -- and the same underlying competence concern -- structures obligations across Shas, not just one tractate.

steps.title: Keep the structure visible
steps.translation: An obligation · what departs from the rule.
steps.prompt: What habit does recognizing a recurring exception clause build?
answers: Once you know a pattern from one tractate, you can recognize its reappearance elsewhere instead of treating it as brand new each time.
Every single tractate must always be learned entirely on its own terms, as if no other tractate anywhere else exists at all.
Recognizing a familiar pattern here means that you are now free to simply stop reading the remaining details closely.
steps.feedback: Good. Recognizing a recurring structure is real transfer -- the skill compounds across tractates.

steps.title: Why these three, specifically
steps.translation: Legal competence (da'at) · obligation.
steps.prompt: What single underlying idea explains why these three, specifically, are the ones excluded?
answers: All three were seen to lack the reliable legal competence (da'at) that an obligation presupposes, so one shared reason excuses them wherever the clause appears.
The three were simply the categories of people who were least likely to be able to afford the long journey up to the Temple in Jerusalem.
They were grouped together here only because all three of them happen to be mentioned side by side within a single verse of the Torah.
steps.feedback: Right. The shared thread is da'at -- reliable legal competence. Because an obligation presupposes it, the same three-way exclusion recurs across Shas wherever competence is the hinge.

steps.title: Recall, don't just recognize
steps.translation: a minor.
steps.prompt: Type the English meaning of קָטָן (katan) from memory, in a word or two.
steps.feedback: Typing it from memory beats recognizing it. The katan -- 'a minor' -- is the third member of the cheresh/shoteh/katan clause, all excluded for the same reason: they lack full da'at.

labs.focus: Read a Mishnah about substitute language by asking what makes an utterance legally binding.

steps.title: Substitute words, real effect
steps.translation: All substitute terms for vows are like vows.
steps.prompt: What does the Mishnah establish about non-standard vow language?
answers: A euphemism or substitute term for the formal vow-word still creates a binding vow.
Only the exact formal word creates any legal effect.
Substitute language cancels the vow entirely, since legal precision failed.
steps.feedback: Right. The Mishnah opens by widening, not narrowing, what counts as effective vow-language.

steps.title: What actually makes language binding
steps.translation: His heart and his mouth are in agreement.
steps.prompt: What principle explains why a substitute term works just as well as the formal one?
answers: Binding force comes from clearly expressed intent, not from reciting one exact required formula.
Only the Sages' precise formula has any legal power, regardless of intent.
Intent is irrelevant to a vow — only the spoken formula itself carries force.
