steps.feedback: Exactly. Once intent is clearly expressed and understood, the exact wording used becomes secondary.

steps.title: Keep the structure visible
steps.translation: A substitute term · a vow.
steps.prompt: What reading habit does this opening reward?
answers: Ask what function a term performs -- creating binding obligation -- rather than requiring it to match one fixed form exactly.
Assume only technically precise legal formulas ever matter in Jewish law.
Treat any variation from the fixed wording as automatically invalidating the legal act.
steps.feedback: Good. Function-over-form is a real, recurring principle worth recognizing when it appears.

steps.title: Where did the substitute words come from?
steps.hebrew: לְשׁוֹן אוּמּוֹת · לָשׁוֹן שֶׁבָּדוּ לָהֶם חֲכָמִים
steps.translation: The language of the nations · language the sages devised.
steps.prompt: The Gemara records a dispute about what kinuyim actually are: Rabbi Yochanan says foreign-influenced forms of the vow-words; Reish Lakish says terms the sages themselves coined. What is at stake in a dispute about origins?
answers: Whether binding vow-language grows from how people actually speak, or is deliberately constructed by the tradition's own authorities.
Whether vows spoken in any language other than Hebrew can ever carry binding legal force at all.
Which of the two sages had the better command of the surrounding nations' languages.
steps.feedback: Good. The dispute is about where effective legal language comes from — usage or enactment — a question that echoes far beyond vows.

steps.title: The Mishnah permits a strange vow
steps.translation: One may vow to murderers, robbers, and tax collectors.
steps.prompt: Later in the tractate, the Mishnah permits declaring a false vow to escape murderers, robbers — and tax collectors. The Gemara objects: but the law of the kingdom is law! What makes the objection powerful?
answers: Grouping tax collectors with robbers seems to deny the state's legitimate authority, which Shmuel's principle explicitly affirms.
The objection shows that vows can never be used defensively, whatever the danger involved.
The Gemara is challenging whether murderers and robbers are really equivalent to each other.
steps.feedback: Exactly. If dina d'malkhuta dina grants lawful taxation real halakhic force, the Mishnah cannot casually treat the collector as a bandit — something must distinguish this collector.

steps.title: Which collector may be evaded
steps.translation: A collector who has no fixed rate.
steps.prompt: The Gemara answers: the Mishnah means a collector with no fixed rate — or one self-appointed rather than commissioned by the kingdom. What does this resolution teach about the principle itself?
answers: The law of the kingdom covers lawful, bounded taxation — arbitrary or unauthorized collection falls outside it, so the exception maps the principle's exact shape.
The principle applies only in cases where the kingdom's own officials personally supervise each individual collection.
The resolution quietly withdraws the principle, since any collector can be suspected of arbitrariness.
steps.feedback: Right. You met this principle as a charter of encounter; here you see its legal machinery — the boundary between law and extortion is exactly where the principle's meaning lives.

steps.title: Recall, don't just recognize
steps.translation: All substitute terms for vows are like vows.
steps.prompt: Type the English meaning of this opening line from memory, in a few words.
acceptable: all substitute terms for vows are like vows
all substitutes for vows are like vows
all nicknames for vows are like vows
substitute terms for vows are like vows
steps.feedback: Typing an answer from memory is a stronger test of durable mastery than recognizing it among choices.

steps.title: Vows are live practice
steps.translation: To learn · to understand · to ask.
steps.prompt: Vows remain a real halakhic institution, with real procedures for release. What is Seder's role here?
answers: Support careful study of how vow-language works while directing any real vow — making one, or seeking release from one — to a qualified rabbinic authority.
Equip learners to judge for themselves whether their own past statements constituted binding vows.
Avoid studying the tractate entirely, since the subject of vows still carries real practical consequences today.
steps.feedback: Right. The tractate's own seriousness about language is the best argument for not treating this lab as personal guidance.

labs.focus: Transfer a principle from Nedarim to a neighboring tractate that opens with the identical structure.

steps.title: A familiar opening, a new status
steps.translation: All substitute terms for nazirite vows are like nazirite vows.
steps.prompt: What does the Mishnah establish here?
answers: A substitute or euphemistic term for accepting nazirite status is just as binding as the exact formal word.
Only the precise word "nazir" itself, and no substitute or euphemism for it, has any binding legal effect.
Nazirite status can never be validly accepted through a spoken declaration of any kind at all.
steps.feedback: Right. This is the same functional principle as Nedarim's opening, applied to a different legal status.

steps.title: You already learned this move
steps.translation: All substitute terms for vows are like vows.
steps.prompt: Nedarim opened with the identical structure applied to ordinary vows. What does that transfer teach you here?
answers: The same function-over-form principle -- clear intent matters more than exact formula -- structures more than one area of Jewish law.
The two tractates must therefore be describing one and the same legal status under two different names.
Nothing at all carries over between neighboring tractates, even when they open with identical wording.
steps.feedback: Exactly. Recognizing the same structural move in a new tractate is what real transfer looks like.

steps.title: Three restrictions define the nazirite
steps.translation: From wine · from cutting the hair · from corpse impurity.
steps.prompt: The status a nazirite accepts (Numbers 6) carries three concrete restrictions: no wine or grape products, no cutting the hair, no contact with the dead. Why does the tractate spend chapters on how the vow is worded before reaching these?
answers: Because the binding word comes first — the restrictions only take hold once a valid acceptance has been established.
Because the three restrictions are optional, and only the wording of the vow is truly required.
Because the wording and the restrictions are unrelated topics the tractate happens to combine.
steps.feedback: Good. Form of acceptance, then content of the status — the Mishnah's order mirrors the logic: nothing is forbidden until the vow validly takes effect.

steps.title: How long, when unspecified
steps.translation: An unspecified nazirite vow is thirty days.
steps.prompt: If someone accepts nazirite status without naming a length, the vow runs thirty days. What kind of legal move is supplying a default?
answers: Filling a gap the speaker left open with a fixed measure, so an incomplete vow still has definite legal content.
Voiding the vow entirely, on the grounds that a vow without a stated length simply cannot take legal effect.
Leaving the length open for the person to decide at some later point, whenever they eventually choose to.
steps.feedback: Right. Law routinely supplies a default for what a person left unspecified — the vow is neither void nor open-ended; it is thirty days.

steps.title: Recall, don't just recognize
steps.translation: All substitute terms for nazirite vows are like nazirite vows.
steps.prompt: Type the English meaning of this opening line from memory, in a few words.
acceptable: all substitute terms for nazirite vows are like nazirite vows
all substitutes for nazirite vows are like nazirite vows
all nicknames for nazirite vows are like nazirite vows
substitute terms for nazirite vows are like nazirite vows
steps.feedback: Typing an answer from memory is a stronger test of durable mastery than recognizing it among choices.

steps.title: A real status, not a game
steps.translation: To learn · to understand · to ask.
steps.prompt: Nazirite status carries real, ongoing practical restrictions once accepted. What is Seder's role here?
answers: Support careful study of the structure and reasoning while directing any real question about accepting or ending nazirite status to a qualified rabbinic authority.
Treat this single Mishnah as sufficient practical guidance for someone who is actually considering taking on such a binding vow themselves.
Avoid studying the tractate at all, on the grounds that a subject still carrying real practical consequences today is unsafe to learn.
steps.feedback: Right. A vow's real consequences are exactly why casual application of this Mishnah alone would be irresponsible.

labs.focus: Read a sensitive tractate's opening procedure with careful attention to its formal legal structure.

steps.title: A formal warning, not an accusation
steps.translation: One who warns his wife.
steps.prompt: What kind of act does the Mishnah's opening word describe?
answers: A formal, procedural warning -- a specific legal act with defined requirements, not a casual suspicion.
An immediate and final legal conclusion, reached before any formal process begins.
An informal act of suspicion carrying no procedural requirements at all.
steps.feedback: Right. The Mishnah is describing a precise legal procedure with formal steps, not a vague accusation.

steps.title: A structural safeguard
steps.translation: On the basis of two [witnesses].
steps.prompt: What does requiring two witnesses for the formal warning accomplish?
answers: It builds a real evidentiary safeguard into the procedure from its very first step, before anything else can follow.
It carries no real legal function and serves a purely ceremonial role in the procedure.
It replaces the need for any further process once the warning has been delivered.
steps.feedback: Exactly. Procedural safeguards like a two-witness requirement are where careful legal reading matters most.

steps.title: Before procedure, a meditation
steps.hebrew: אַרְבָּעִים יוֹם קוֹדֶם יְצִירַת הַוָּלָד בַּת קוֹל יוֹצֵאת וְאוֹמֶרֶת
steps.translation: Forty days before the formation of the child, a heavenly voice goes out and says: the daughter of so-and-so to so-and-so.
steps.prompt: Before analyzing the procedure, the Gemara opens with matches proclaimed in heaven before birth. Why might a painful tractate open this way?
answers: The aggadah frames the legal material: before dissecting a marriage's crisis, the tractate dwells on the bond's depth and mystery.
The opening rules that a heavenly-matched marriage can never actually reach the sotah procedure.
The passage is a displaced fragment that belongs in a tractate about marriage rather than here.
steps.feedback: Good. Aggadah beside halakhah is deliberate architecture — the Gemara sets the weight of what is at stake before a single procedural word.

steps.title: Why Sotah sits beside Nazir
steps.hebrew: כָּל הָרוֹאֶה סוֹטָה בְּקִלְקוּלָהּ יַזִּיר עַצְמוֹ מִן הַיַּיִן
steps.translation: Whoever sees a sotah in her disgrace should take a nazirite vow against wine.
steps.prompt: The Gemara explains the tractate-order: witnessing this procedure's outcome should move a person to swear off wine. What does the explanation assume about learning itself?
answers: That even the arrangement of tractates can teach — proximity to moral collapse is expected to change the onlooker's behavior.
That nazirite vows were legally mandatory for everyone who was present at the procedure.
That the tractates were ordered purely by length, and the explanation is decorative.
steps.feedback: Exactly. The ordering answer is itself a moral claim: seeing consequences should reshape conduct — the canon's very structure carries the lesson.

steps.title: Where walking in His ways lives
steps.hebrew: מָה הוּא מַלְבִּישׁ עֲרוּמִּים אַף אַתָּה הַלְבֵּשׁ עֲרוּמִּים
steps.translation: Just as He clothes the naked, so too you clothe the naked.
steps.prompt: The same tractate later holds Sotah 14a — the classic source that walking after God means imitating His deeds: clothing the naked, visiting the sick, comforting mourners. What does finding it here teach about tractates?
answers: A tractate named for its hardest procedure can hold some of the tradition's most humane teaching — tractates are worlds, not single topics.
The imitation-of-God teaching is meant to apply only within the marital law that surrounds it here.
The passage was placed in this tractate by error, and later editors simply chose not to move it.
steps.feedback: Right. If you came here from the comparative unit on the middle path, this is the sugya it stands on — met now in its own home.

steps.title: Recall, don't just recognize
steps.translation: On the basis of two [witnesses].
steps.prompt: Type the English meaning of this evidentiary phrase from memory, in a few words.
acceptable: on the basis of two witnesses
by the word of two witnesses
on the word of two witnesses
by the mouth of two witnesses
steps.feedback: Typing an answer from memory is a stronger test of durable mastery than recognizing it among choices.

steps.title: Structure, not guidance
steps.translation: To learn · to understand · to ask.
steps.prompt: This tractate addresses deeply personal, halakhically consequential material no longer practiced in its original form. What is Seder's role?
answers: Support careful study of its legal structure and reasoning as a historical and textual subject, while directing any real personal situation to a qualified rabbinic authority.
Use this material as a practical framework for evaluating a real relationship or personal situation in one's own life.
Avoid teaching the tractate's structure at all, since material this painful and personal is better left outside any serious learning curriculum.
steps.feedback: Right. Structural literacy about a historical legal procedure is not the same as personal guidance, and this tractate calls for that distinction more than most.

labs.focus: Trace a Mishnaic legal category back to its Torah source and reciprocal logic.

steps.title: A question about false testimony
steps.translation: How do witnesses become conspiring [false witnesses]?
steps.prompt: What kind of question opens this tractate?
answers: A procedural question about how a specific legal status -- proven false testimony -- is established.
A broad question that the Mishnah leaves open, without any defined legal answer to follow.
A rhetorical flourish with no real legal content behind it, meant only to open the tractate.
steps.feedback: Right. "How" signals a procedural question the Mishnah is about to answer concretely.

steps.title: Where the consequence comes from
steps.hebrew: וַעֲשִׂיתֶם לוֹ כַּאֲשֶׁר זָמַם לַעֲשׂוֹת לְאָחִיו
steps.translation: You shall do to him as he schemed to do to his brother.
steps.prompt: This is the Torah source (Deuteronomy 19:19) behind the Mishnah's category. What principle does it establish?
answers: A reciprocal consequence: the punishment intended for the falsely accused is instead applied to the false witnesses themselves.
A fixed penalty entirely unrelated to whatever the false witnesses had actually alleged against the accused.
A rule that false witnesses, once their testimony is given, are never afterward held accountable for it.
steps.feedback: Exactly. The Mishnah's category is built directly on this reciprocal principle from the Torah's own text.

steps.title: Schemed, not did
steps.translation: As he schemed — and not as he did.
steps.prompt: The Gemara reads the verse's word ‘schemed’ with startling precision: false witnesses receive the punishment only if their plot was exposed BEFORE it was carried out. If the accused was already executed on their word, they are not. What does this close reading reveal?
answers: A single word — ‘schemed’ rather than ‘did’ — sets the exact boundary of the law, so the timing of exposure decides everything.
The law is essentially arbitrary here, punishing some false witnesses and sparing others with no real principle behind it.
The verse offers only a general sentiment, and the precise timing distinction must be drawn from some other source entirely.
steps.feedback: Right. This is the tractate's famous chiddush: the reciprocal law is triggered by the scheme, not its result — one verb carries the whole rule, and reading it closely is the skill.

steps.title: Refuting the witness, not the fact
steps.translation: Refutation-by-alibi · not mere contradiction.
steps.prompt: The reciprocal law applies only through hazama — a second pair testifying ‘you two were with US elsewhere, so you could not have seen this.’ Plain hakhasha, where a second pair simply says the event did not happen, does not trigger it. Why does the distinction matter so much?
answers: Hazama attacks the witnesses' presence, exposing them as liars; hakhasha only pits fact against fact, leaving no way to know who erred.
The two terms are interchangeable, and the tractate uses both names for the very same act of refutation.
Hakhasha is the stronger refutation, so it, rather than hazama, is what triggers the reciprocal punishment.
steps.feedback: Exactly. Only discrediting the witnesses themselves — not disputing the facts — makes them provably false, which is what the verse's ‘as he schemed’ requires.

steps.title: Keep the structure visible
steps.translation: Testimony · scheme · consequence.
steps.prompt: What habit does tracing a Mishnaic category back to its verse reward?
answers: A Mishnaic legal category is rarely invented from nothing -- tracing it to its Torah source clarifies exactly why it works the way it does.
Torah verses and Mishnaic legal categories are always entirely unrelated to each other.
Once a category has been named, the Torah source it rests on becomes irrelevant.
steps.feedback: Good. This source-tracing habit -- practiced already in Bava Kamma and elsewhere -- applies here too.

steps.title: Recall, don't just recognize
steps.translation: As he schemed to do to his brother.
steps.prompt: Type the English meaning of this phrase — the Torah source of the whole category — from memory.
acceptable: as he schemed to do to his brother
as he plotted to do to his brother
as he intended to do to his brother
as he schemed to do to his fellow
as he conspired to do to his brother
steps.feedback: Typing an answer from memory is a stronger test of durable mastery than recognizing it among choices.

labs.focus: Recognize an opening grammatical pattern shared with a tractate you have already studied.

steps.title: A familiar counting pattern
steps.translation: Oaths: two that are four.
steps.prompt: What kind of opening structure does this Mishnah use?
answers: A counted opening: two basic categories that expand into four total cases.
A single, uncategorized ruling stated on its own with no breakdown into cases.
A narrative passage that carries no legal categories or counting at all.
steps.feedback: Right. This is a counted opening -- the same shape you have seen used to organize a legal field before it is spelled out case by case.

steps.title: The exact same phrase, a different subject
steps.translation: The acts of carrying out on Shabbat are two that are four.
steps.prompt: You already read this identical phrase pattern in Shabbat's opening Mishnah. What does recognizing it here do for you?
answers: It lets you immediately expect a counted field of basic-plus-extended cases, before reading a single detail of the oaths themselves.
It proves that oaths and the Shabbat labor of carrying must belong to one and the same underlying legal category.
It means the two tractates that share this phrase must have been composed and edited by the very same author.
steps.feedback: Exactly. The Mishnah itself uses this "two that are four" phrase across several tractates -- recognizing the shape lets you read new content faster.

steps.title: What the two and the four actually are
steps.hebrew: אֹכַל · לֹא אֹכַל · אָכַלְתִּי · לֹא אָכַלְתִּי
steps.translation: I will eat · I will not eat · I ate · I did not eat.
steps.prompt: For an oath of utterance, the ‘two’ are a positive and a negative oath; the ‘four’ come from applying each to the future and the past. What does spelling out the four teach about the counting phrase?
answers: The Torah states two (future oaths); the sages extend the same logic to the past, so ‘two that are four’ names a real derivation, not just a tally.
The four cases are four wholly unrelated kinds of oath that happen to be grouped together here by their number alone.
The phrase is purely rhetorical flourish, and in reality there are only ever two oaths in every single instance.
steps.feedback: Good. Two Torah cases (‘I will’ / ‘I will not’) plus their past-tense counterparts make four — the count encodes how the Oral Law extends a written pair.

steps.title: Keep the structure visible
steps.translation: Two · four.
steps.prompt: What habit does recognizing a shared opening pattern across tractates build?
answers: A grammatical or structural pattern is worth learning on its own, since it will recur in unrelated legal subjects.
Every new Mishnah must be approached from scratch, as if no structural pattern could ever repeat across tractates.
Structural patterns like this one only ever matter within the single tractate where you first meet them.
steps.feedback: Good. This is the same discoverable-pattern skill this session's cross-tractate work has built again and again.

steps.title: Recall, don't just recognize
steps.translation: Oaths: two that are four.
steps.prompt: Type the English meaning of this opening line from memory, in a few words.
acceptable: oaths two that they are four
steps.feedback: Typing an answer from memory is a stronger test of durable mastery than recognizing it among choices.

labs.focus: Read a Mishnah about trusting institutional authority, and its limits.

steps.title: A court's own error
steps.hebrew: הוֹרוּ בֵית דִּין לַעֲבוֹר עַל אַחַת מִכָּל מִצְוֹת הָאֲמוּרוֹת בַּתּוֹרָה
steps.translation: A court issued a ruling permitting the violation of one of the Torah's commandments.
steps.prompt: What situation does the Mishnah address first?
answers: A case where the highest legal authority itself made an error, and an individual relied on it in good faith.
A carefully bounded case constructed so that no institutional error is even possible in the first place.
A case about an individual who acts entirely on his own, with no court or ruling involved at all.
steps.feedback: Right. The Mishnah opens by directly confronting the possibility that even a court can rule incorrectly.

steps.title: Why reliance matters
steps.translation: Exempt, because he relied on the court.
steps.prompt: What does this exemption reveal about how the Mishnah treats institutional trust?
answers: Good-faith reliance on a properly constituted legal authority is itself legally significant, even when that authority turns out to have erred.
Relying on a court's ruling never carries any legal weight at all, whatever the circumstances of the reliance.
The individual remains fully liable for the transgression regardless of what the court had actually ruled.
steps.feedback: Exactly. This is the same question the Oven of Akhnai aggada raises from a different angle -- what legitimate authority a properly constituted process carries, even when imperfect.

steps.title: The scholar who knew better
steps.hebrew: חַיָּב מִפְּנֵי שֶׁלֹּא תָלָה בְּבֵית דִּין
steps.translation: Liable, because he did not [really] rely on the court.
steps.prompt: The Mishnah adds a striking exception: a scholar who recognized the court had erred, yet followed the ruling anyway, is liable. Why does the same act — obeying the court — exempt one person and condemn another?
answers: The exemption rests on genuine reliance; one who saw the error did not truly rely, so his obedience was his own choice and his own responsibility.
The scholar is liable here only because scholars are always held to a stricter and harsher legal standard than ordinary people are.
The scholar is liable because the act of following any court ruling at all is itself treated by the law as a kind of transgression.
steps.feedback: Right. The law protects good-faith reliance, not blind obedience — knowing the ruling was wrong dissolves the very reliance that would have exempted him.

steps.title: An offering for an institution's mistake
steps.translation: A bull for a matter hidden from the community.
steps.prompt: When the high court errs and most of the people follow, the community as a whole brings a special offering — the par he'elem davar. What does having a dedicated communal offering reveal?
answers: The system anticipates that institutions themselves can err collectively, and builds a formal, corporate way to acknowledge and repair it.
The offering exists to shift all of the blame onto the individuals who acted, sparing the court any acknowledgment of its error.
The offering is a purely theoretical construct that was never actually connected to any real institutional mistake in practice.
steps.feedback: Exactly. A named offering for institutional error is a remarkable admission built into the law: even the highest court is fallible, and the repair is communal, not hidden.

steps.title: Recall, don't just recognize
steps.translation: Exempt, because he relied on the court.
steps.prompt: Type the English meaning of this exemption from memory, in a few words.
acceptable: exempt because he relied on the court
exempt because he relied on the court
exempt for he relied on the court
exempt since he relied on the court
exempt because he depended on the court
steps.feedback: Typing an answer from memory is a stronger test of durable mastery than recognizing it among choices.

steps.title: Institutional trust has limits
steps.translation: To learn · to understand · to ask.
steps.prompt: What is the responsible takeaway from a Mishnah about trusting institutional rulings?
answers: Good-faith reliance on a qualified authority is meaningful, but this Mishnah is about a specific ancient court structure -- not a license to treat any claimed authority as automatically binding today.
Any ruling from any source should be followed without question.
Institutional authority described in this Mishnah has no relevance to anything today.
steps.feedback: Right. Recognizing what made a court's authority legitimate is itself part of reading this Mishnah responsibly.

labs.focus: Read an opening Mishnah about intention by tracking exactly what a flawed intention does and does not undo.

steps.title: An offering, an intention problem
steps.translation: All offerings that were slaughtered not for their own designated purpose.
steps.prompt: What kind of problem does the Mishnah open with?
answers: A mismatch between the intention behind an act and the offering's designated purpose.
A physical defect or blemish found in the sacrificial animal itself.
A problem with the timing of the act that has nothing to do with intention.
steps.feedback: Right. This Mishnah is about the role intention plays in a ritual act, not the physical object itself.

steps.title: Valid, but incomplete
steps.hebrew: כְּשֵׁרוֹת אֶלָּא שֶׁלֹּא עָלוּ לַבְּעָלִים לְשֵׁם חוֹבָה
steps.translation: Valid, but they do not count for the owners as fulfilling their obligation.
steps.prompt: What does this two-part outcome reveal about how the Mishnah weighs a flawed intention?
answers: A flawed intention can leave an act technically valid while still failing to accomplish its full legal purpose -- two separate questions.
A flawed intention always completely and fully invalidates the whole act it accompanies, no matter the surrounding circumstances.
The intention behind the act has no real bearing whatsoever on its final outcome or on its resulting legal standing at all.
steps.feedback: Exactly. Separating "is it valid" from "did it accomplish its purpose" is a real analytical move this Mishnah teaches.

steps.title: Keep the structure visible
steps.translation: For its designated purpose · validity · obligation.
steps.prompt: What reading habit does this opening reward?
answers: Track intention, validity, and obligation-fulfillment as three separate questions that do not always move together.
Assume that any flaw in intention will always produce the exact same legal outcome every single time.
Skip past all questions about intention, on the assumption that only the physical act itself matters.
steps.feedback: Good. This three-part distinction recurs throughout Seder Kodashim.

steps.title: Two offerings that intention can void
steps.translation: Except for the Passover offering and the sin offering.
steps.prompt: The Mishnah names two offerings — pesach and chatat — that ARE invalidated when slaughtered with the wrong intention. Why would these two differ from every other offering?
answers: Both are defined by a fixed purpose the Torah ties them to — atonement, or the Passover night — so a different purpose strikes at what they essentially are.
Because these two particular offerings are simply more important than all the others and so are judged by a stricter standard.
Because the pesach and the chatat are the only two offerings that a private individual would ever have occasion to bring.
steps.feedback: Right. Where an offering's whole identity is bound to one purpose, wrong-purpose intent does not merely fail to credit the owner — it unmakes the act. The lishmah requirement you met in Gittin returns here in sacrificial form.

steps.title: Recall, don't just recognize
steps.translation: Not for their own designated purpose.
steps.prompt: Type the English meaning of this phrase — the intention flaw the whole Mishnah turns on — from memory.
acceptable: not for their own designated purpose
steps.feedback: Typing an answer from memory is a stronger test of durable mastery than recognizing it among choices.

labs.focus: Transfer Zevachim's intention analysis to a parallel opening about meal-offerings.

steps.title: The same problem, a different offering
steps.translation: All meal-offerings from which a handful was taken not for their own designated purpose.
steps.prompt: What does this opening line do?
answers: It applies the identical intention-versus-validity question from Zevachim to meal-offerings instead of animal-offerings.
It introduces a completely unrelated legal problem that bears no connection to anything studied in Zevachim earlier.
It simply repeats the Zevachim case about slaughtered animals word for word, with nothing at all changed or added.
steps.feedback: Right. Menachot deliberately opens as a structural parallel to Zevachim, applied to a different category of offering.

steps.title: Valid, but incomplete -- again
steps.hebrew: כְּשֵׁרוֹת אֶלָּא שֶׁלֹּא עָלוּ לַבְּעָלִים לְשֵׁם חוֹבָה
steps.translation: Valid, but they do not count for the owners as fulfilling their obligation.
steps.prompt: What does recognizing this repeated conclusion let you do?
answers: Apply the same validity-versus-obligation distinction learned in Zevachim immediately, without re-deriving it from scratch.
Assume that meal-offerings and animal-offerings must be legally identical in every last respect, with no differences at all.
Ignore the specific exceptions that Menachot raises, on the grounds that Zevachim has already settled every possible case.
steps.feedback: Exactly. Real transfer means applying an already-learned distinction to new material efficiently -- while still watching for where the parallel breaks down.

steps.title: Two offerings the parallel does not cover
steps.translation: Except for the sinner's meal-offering and the jealousy (sotah) meal-offering.
steps.prompt: The Mishnah carves out two meal-offerings that a wrong intention actually invalidates. What links these two?
answers: Each is tied to one fixed purpose -- atoning for a sin, or testing a suspicion -- so a wrong intention strikes at what it essentially is.
They are simply the two most costly and valuable meal-offerings brought in the Temple, so the Mishnah holds them to a stricter rule.
They are the only two meal-offerings that an ordinary private individual would ever actually have any occasion to bring at all.
steps.feedback: Right. This mirrors Zevachim's pesach and chatat exactly: where an offering's whole identity is bound to one purpose, doing it for another purpose invalidates it -- the same move you named in the Zevachim lab.

steps.title: Keep the structure visible
steps.translation: For its designated purpose · validity · obligation.
steps.prompt: What should a careful reader still check, even with a strong parallel like this one?
answers: Where Menachot's own stated exceptions differ from Zevachim's, since a parallel structure does not guarantee identical content.
Nothing further at all, because once a parallel between two tractates is established no additional reading is ever really needed.
Only whether the two tractates happen to have been composed and edited during one and the same historical period long ago.
steps.feedback: Good. Transfer speeds up reading; it should never replace checking the specific text in front of you.

steps.title: Recall, don't just recognize
steps.translation: not for their own sake.
steps.prompt: Type the English meaning of the phrase שֶׁלֹּא לִשְׁמָן (shelo lishman) from memory, in a few words.
steps.feedback: Typing it from memory is a stronger test of durable mastery than picking it from a list. Shelo lishman -- 'not for its own sake' -- is the single hinge concept that Zevachim and Menachot share.

labs.focus: Read a Mishnah about ownership and obligation by tracking exactly when a status attaches.

steps.title: A transaction, a question of ownership
steps.translation: One who purchases the unborn fetus of a donkey belonging to a non-Jew.
steps.prompt: What kind of situation opens this tractate?
answers: A transaction whose ownership history determines whether a later legal obligation applies at all.
A transaction that has no real bearing on whether any later legal obligation would ever come to apply.
A case demonstrating that the timing of ownership never actually matters to how Jewish law is applied.
steps.feedback: Right. The Mishnah opens with a transaction precisely because the obligation in question depends on ownership timing.

steps.title: When the obligation attaches
steps.translation: Exempt from the firstborn obligation.
steps.prompt: What does this exemption reveal about when the firstborn-animal obligation attaches?
answers: The obligation depends on the animal being owned by a Jew at the relevant moment, not merely on its eventual owner.
Ownership plays no role whatsoever in the matter; only the animal's underlying biological status ever counts here.
The firstborn obligation applies automatically to every such animal, regardless of who owned it or exactly when.
steps.feedback: Exactly. Tracking exactly which moment of ownership triggers a legal status is the core skill this Mishnah teaches.

steps.title: Why even a partial stake matters
steps.translation: A non-Jew's partnership exempts the animal from the firstborn obligation.
steps.prompt: Why does even a non-Jew's partial share in the animal remove the firstborn obligation entirely?
answers: Firstborn sanctity attaches only to an animal wholly owned by a Jew, so any outside share in it blocks the status from arising.
Because a firstborn animal that is jointly owned by two parties is always divided evenly, and the non-Jew simply keeps his own half.
Because the obligation is really just a financial debt that the non-Jewish partner is expected to pay off on the owner's behalf.
steps.feedback: Right. The status is all-or-nothing: it needs full Jewish ownership at the triggering moment, so a partial outside stake keeps it from ever attaching.

steps.title: Keep the structure visible
steps.translation: Acquisition · a moment · an obligation.
steps.prompt: What reading habit does this case reward?
answers: Ask exactly which moment in a sequence of events triggers a legal obligation, rather than assuming that obligation holds constant throughout.
Assume that every ownership transaction of this general kind carries the exact same legal consequences every single time.
Treat all questions about the timing of ownership as essentially irrelevant to the religious obligations that are at stake.
steps.feedback: Good. Precision about timing is what turns a transaction into a legal question with a real answer.

steps.title: Recall, don't just recognize
steps.translation: exempt from the firstborn obligation.
steps.prompt: Type the English meaning of the word פָּטוּר (patur) from memory.
steps.feedback: Typing it from memory beats picking it from a list. Patur -- 'exempt' -- is the pivot word: the whole Mishnah turns on when the firstborn obligation does and does not attach.

labs.focus: Read a Mishnah about a fixed-value vow system grounded in its Torah source.

steps.title: A vow with a fixed answer
steps.translation: All may vow another's valuation, and all may have their valuation vowed.
steps.prompt: What kind of vow does this Mishnah describe?
answers: A vow whose amount is not decided by the person vowing, but fixed in advance by category (such as age) according to the Torah.
A vow whose amount is left entirely open to free negotiation between the two parties who are involved in it.
A vow that carries no real financial content or monetary obligation of any binding kind whatsoever at all.
steps.feedback: Right. An "arakhin" vow is unusual precisely because its value is pre-set, not chosen.

steps.title: Where the fixed values come from
steps.translation: Then your valuation shall be.
steps.prompt: This phrase, from Leviticus 27, is the Torah source behind the Mishnah's system. What does grounding the Mishnah in this verse accomplish?
answers: It shows the fixed-value structure is not a later rabbinic invention, but built directly on the Torah's own valuation table.
It proves that the Mishnah here has invented an entirely new financial system resting on no prior textual basis.
It shows that the cited verse and the Mishnah's rule are in fact wholly unrelated to one another in the end.
steps.feedback: Exactly. Tracing a Mishnaic system back to its Torah source is what turns a curious rule into a grounded one.

steps.title: Keep the structure visible
steps.translation: A vow · a valuation · Torah.
steps.prompt: What habit does tracing this system to its source reward?
answers: Ask whether an unusual-seeming Mishnaic structure has a direct Torah source before assuming it is arbitrary.
Assume that every unusual-seeming rule found in the Mishnah must be a later addition carrying no biblical basis at all.
Skip checking the Torah source entirely, on the assumption that the Mishnah's own text by itself is always sufficient.
steps.feedback: Good. This source-tracing habit applies as much in Kodashim as it does anywhere else in Shas.

steps.title: Fixed value, not market value
steps.translation: A fixed valuation · [market] value.
steps.prompt: How does an erech vow differ from a vow to donate a person's 'value' (damim)?
answers: An erech uses the Torah's fixed schedule by age and sex, ignoring the individual's actual worth; a damim vow is assessed by real market value.
An erech vow and a damim vow are really just two different names for the very same fixed-schedule calculation used in each case.
An erech is paid out in produce while a damim vow is always paid in silver coins, though the assessed amount itself is identical.
steps.feedback: Right. The erech's whole character is that it is fixed in advance -- the same age and sex always yields the same amount, regardless of the actual person.

steps.title: Recall, don't just recognize
steps.translation: a fixed valuation.
steps.prompt: Type the English meaning of עֵרֶךְ (erech) from memory, in a word or two.
steps.feedback: Typing it from memory beats recognizing it. Erech -- a 'valuation' set in advance by the Torah's table -- is the concept the whole tractate is built on.

labs.focus: Read a genuine legal paradox: an act that is forbidden yet still legally effective.

steps.title: A forbidden act, stated plainly
steps.translation: All may substitute [a consecrated animal for another].
steps.prompt: What does the Mishnah's opening word suggest about who can perform this act?
answers: The act of substitution is broadly possible to perform, even though (as the tractate will show) it is forbidden to do so.
Only a small number of specially authorized individuals are ever permitted to attempt performing this act at all.
The act being described here is one that is entirely permitted, carrying with it no legal restriction of any kind.
steps.feedback: Right. "All may" describes legal capability, not permission -- a distinction this tractate depends on.

steps.title: Forbidden, yet it takes effect
steps.translation: It and its substitute shall be holy.
steps.prompt: What does this Torah-grounded outcome reveal about the act of substitution?
answers: The act is forbidden and punishable, yet it still legally succeeds -- both animals become consecrated despite the prohibition.
The forbidden act of substitution simply fails outright to produce any binding legal effect whatsoever once attempted.
Only the original consecrated animal keeps its holiness, while the substitute animal stays entirely ordinary and unholy.
steps.feedback: Exactly. This is a genuine paradox: violating the law does not undo the legal reality the law itself creates.

steps.title: Keep the structure visible
steps.translation: Prohibition · legal effect.
steps.prompt: What reading habit does a paradox like this reward?
answers: Ask separately whether an act is permitted and whether it is legally effective -- the law sometimes answers these two questions differently.
Assume that a forbidden act can never carry any real or lasting legal consequence at all once it has been done.
Treat every prohibition as though it automatically voids and undoes whatever legal result that act produced.
steps.feedback: Good. Separating permission from effect is a precise, transferable distinction.

steps.title: Why both animals end up holy
steps.translation: A sanctity that does not lapse [on command].
steps.prompt: Why do BOTH animals end up holy, rather than the sanctity simply moving over to the substitute?
answers: A person's word cannot strip sanctity off the first animal, so the attempt to swap it only adds sanctity to the second -- both are now holy.
The Torah rewards the act of substitution by doubling the sanctity, deliberately granting holiness to each of the two animals as a bonus.
The two animals are treated as one single combined offering, so any holiness naming just one of them will automatically cover both.
steps.feedback: Right. Sanctity here is sticky -- it will not detach on command -- so a forbidden swap cannot subtract it, only extend it. That is the paradox's engine.

steps.title: Recall, don't just recognize
steps.translation: a substitute.
steps.prompt: Type the English meaning of תְּמוּרָה (temurah) from memory, in a word or two.
steps.feedback: Typing it from memory beats recognizing it. Temurah -- a 'substitute' -- names both the forbidden act and the animal it produces, the pair the whole paradox turns on.

labs.focus: Read a counted Mishnah that opens by surveying an entire category across the Torah.

steps.title: A count across the whole Torah
steps.translation: Thirty-six [transgressions carrying the penalty of] karet in the Torah.
steps.prompt: What kind of opening does this Mishnah provide?
answers: A complete survey, gathering a single category of consequence from across the entire Torah into one count.
A single isolated case that bears essentially no relationship at all to the wider body of the Torah's laws.
An open-ended and essentially uncountable topic, one carrying no defined boundaries or limits of any kind.
steps.feedback: Right. A precise count like this signals the Mishnah is organizing material scattered across many places into one field.

steps.title: What separates these cases
steps.translation: Excision [karet].
steps.prompt: What does grouping these cases under one consequence, karet, actually track?
answers: A specific category of deliberate, uncorrected violation -- distinguished from cases handled through an offering for an unwitting sin.
Any violation of absolutely any kind at all, whether it happened to be done deliberately or else entirely by accident.
A punishment that is reserved solely for violations committed against other people, and never for those against God.
steps.feedback: Exactly. Karet marks a specific category -- and the count exists because the Torah's language for it varies across many different laws.

steps.title: Keep the structure visible
steps.translation: A count · a category.
steps.prompt: What reading habit does a Torah-wide count like this reward?
answers: Recognize that one legal category can be scattered across many different verses, and a Mishnah may exist specifically to gather them.
Assume that every distinct legal category must always be stated in exactly one single identifiable place in the Torah.
Skip right past counted openings like this one, on the assumption that the number itself simply carries no information.
steps.feedback: Good. A count is itself a claim worth taking seriously -- ask what it is counting and why.

steps.title: Why the count exists
steps.translation: Its deliberate form: karet · its unwitting form: a sin-offering.
steps.prompt: The Mishnah pairs karet with a second consequence. What systematic link does it draw?
answers: For most of these deliberate karet sins, doing the same act unwittingly instead obligates a chatat offering -- one sin, two versions.
Each of these karet sins is separately paired with a matching monetary fine, one payable to the Temple treasury in every case.
Karet is said to apply only where no offering was ever brought, so this count simply lists the sins that have no atonement path.
steps.feedback: Right. Keritot's organizing idea: the deliberate, karet-bearing version and the unwitting, chatat-bearing version are two faces of one prohibition -- the count sets up that pairing.

steps.title: Recall, don't just recognize
steps.translation: excision; being cut off.
steps.prompt: Type the English meaning of כָּרֵת (karet) from memory, in a few words.
acceptable: being cut off from the people
being cut off from the community
steps.feedback: Typing it from memory beats recognizing it. Karet -- 'excision', being cut off -- is the single consequence whose thirty-six instances this whole tractate gathers and counts.

labs.focus: Read a Mishnah distinguishing an offering's ritual validity from its sanctity status.

steps.title: A disqualified offering, still consecrated
steps.translation: Offerings of the most sacred order that were slaughtered in the south [of the courtyard].
steps.prompt: What kind of problem does this Mishnah address?
answers: An offering became ritually disqualified through a procedural error, and the question is what that does and does not change.
An offering that carries no procedural issue or ritual defect of any kind at all in the first place here.
A case that bears no genuine relationship to the laws of Temple procedure whatsoever in the end.
steps.feedback: Right. A wrong location is exactly the kind of procedural flaw that raises a real legal question about what changes and what doesn't.

steps.title: Disqualified, but still sacred
steps.translation: One transgresses through misappropriation regarding them.
steps.prompt: What does this outcome reveal about the relationship between validity and sanctity?
answers: An offering can lose its ritual validity for the service while its sanctity -- and the ban on misusing it -- remains fully intact.
Losing ritual validity here always means that the offering loses its underlying sanctity right along with it too.
Sanctity and validity are really just one and the same single status, simply referred to under two different names.
steps.feedback: Exactly. This Mishnah teaches that validity and sanctity are two separate questions, not one -- a flaw in one does not automatically erase the other.

steps.title: Keep the structure visible
steps.translation: Validity · sanctity.
steps.prompt: What reading habit does this distinction reward?
answers: When a status seems to fail, ask which one failed -- validity for its use, sanctity itself, or both -- rather than assuming one implies the other.
Assume that any procedural flaw at all must automatically erase every single status that is connected to the object.
Treat the two terms validity and sanctity as though they were simply fully interchangeable with each other.
steps.feedback: Good. This same disciplined separation of related-but-distinct statuses recurs across Seder Kodashim.

steps.title: What the liability actually means
steps.translation: Misappropriation of sacred property.
steps.prompt: Given that the disqualified offering is still sacred, what does 'one transgresses through me'ilah' practically mean here?
answers: Using this offering for ordinary benefit is still me'ilah -- misuse of sacred property -- since the sanctity that triggers that liability never left it.
Since the offering has been disqualified, using it now for ordinary personal benefit is fully permitted and carries no liability at all.
The phrase means that only the priests may still benefit from it, and any layperson who uses it owes a fixed monetary penalty.
steps.feedback: Right. Me'ilah -- misappropriating hekdesh -- is triggered by sanctity, not by validity, so a flawed but still-sacred offering keeps its me'ilah liability fully.

steps.title: Recall, don't just recognize
steps.translation: misappropriation of sacred property.
steps.prompt: Type the English meaning of מְעִילָה (me'ilah) from memory, in a few words.
steps.feedback: Typing it from memory beats recognizing it. Me'ilah -- misusing sacred property -- is the liability that survives even when the offering's ritual validity does not.

labs.focus: Read a Mishnah about ceremonial practice by distinguishing its stated reason from a merely practical one.

steps.title: A guard system, named precisely
steps.translation: In three places the priests would stand guard.
steps.prompt: What kind of practice does this Mishnah describe?
answers: A structured, named system of guard posts within the Temple, described with precision.
An informal and unstructured custom that has no fixed positions or defined posts of any sort at all.
A guard system whose underlying purpose is left entirely unstated and effectively unknowable to us.
steps.feedback: Right. Precision about the number and location of posts signals that the practice has a defined structure worth investigating.

steps.title: Not what you might expect
steps.translation: For the sake of the Temple's honor.
steps.prompt: What does this stated reason reveal about the guard system's purpose?
answers: The guards were not mainly protecting against theft -- their presence itself expressed the Temple's honor, whether or not a threat existed.
The guards existed purely and only in order to prevent the theft of the Temple's valuable property and vessels.
The Mishnah offers no stated reason of any kind at all for why this particular guard practice ever existed.
steps.feedback: Exactly. A practical-looking practice can have a primarily ceremonial or dignity-based purpose -- worth checking rather than assuming.

steps.title: Keep the structure visible
steps.translation: A practice · a reason.
steps.prompt: What reading habit does this case reward?
answers: Ask for the stated reason behind a practice rather than assuming the most obvious practical explanation is the real one.
Assume that every guard-like practice of this general sort must exist only in order to prevent theft and nothing else.
Skip looking for the stated reason at all, on the assumption that the practice itself is surely entirely self-explanatory.
steps.feedback: Good. The stated reason is often more interesting, and more revealing, than the assumed one.

steps.title: A tractate with almost no disputes
steps.translation: The order of the daily (tamid) service.
steps.prompt: Tamid is unusual among tractates: it contains almost no disputes. What does that tell you about how to read it?
answers: It is largely a step-by-step narrative of the daily service, so the task is to follow a sequence of actions rather than to weigh opposing opinions.
It means that the tractate must be purely theoretical, describing a Temple service that was in fact never once actually carried out.
It shows that the tractate is incomplete, and that its missing disputes were simply recorded somewhere else in the Talmud instead.
steps.feedback: Right. Tamid mostly narrates the morning service as a sequence -- reading it well means tracking the order of actions, not hunting for a machloket that is not there.

steps.title: Recall, don't just recognize
steps.translation: continual; the daily offering.
steps.prompt: Type the English meaning of תָּמִיד (tamid) from memory, in a word or two.
steps.feedback: Typing it from memory beats recognizing it. Tamid -- 'continual' -- names the twice-daily offering whose ordered service this narrative tractate reconstructs.
